parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why it is important to maintain biodiversity.
parts.answer: Any three: moral/ethical duty to other species and future generations; economic value – food, timber, crops, ecotourism; source of medicines and new genes for crop breeding; ecosystem services – pollination, nutrient recycling, flood control, oxygen; stability of food webs/ecosystems; aesthetic/cultural value.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three different reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Indus river dolphin lives only in the Indus river system and is endangered. Its range is split into sections by barrages built for irrigation. Suggest three threats to this species, other than barrages.
parts.answer: Any three: low water flow in the dry season because water is taken for irrigation; pollution from industry, sewage and agricultural chemicals; accidental capture in fishing nets (bycatch); dolphins stranded in irrigation canals; reduced fish prey from overfishing; noise/boat traffic; small, isolated populations losing genetic diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three suitable threats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how national parks such as Khunjerab National Park help to conserve endangered species.
parts.answer: Habitat is protected from development, farming and logging; hunting is banned or controlled; whole ecosystems are protected, so food chains and interactions are kept; species can be monitored and studied.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: habitat protected; hunting/poaching controlled; whole ecosystem/all species protected; monitoring/research; controlled tourism raises money.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Astola Island became Pakistan's first marine protected area. Suggest two activities that might be restricted in a marine protected area and explain how one of them benefits marine species.
parts.answer: Fishing (especially trawling or net fishing); collecting corals/shells; anchoring boats; dumping waste/pollution; development of the coastline. E.g. banning fishing lets fish populations recover and breed; this provides food for other species and fish spread to surrounding areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two restricted activities. 1 mark for a valid explanation of benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the roles of zoos in the conservation of endangered species such as the snow leopard.
parts.answer: Captive breeding to increase numbers; maintaining genetic diversity using studbooks and exchanging animals between zoos (avoiding inbreeding); reintroduction of animals into the wild; research into behaviour, nutrition and reproduction; education of the public and fund-raising for conservation in the wild; keeping a safe population if wild populations are lost.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: captive breeding; studbooks/exchange to keep genetic diversity; reintroduction; research; education/raising awareness; fund-raising; safe 'reserve' population; assisted reproduction (IVF, AI).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a captive population started from only a few founder animals may have problems after several generations.
parts.answer: Small gene pool / low genetic diversity; inbreeding increases the chance of offspring being homozygous for harmful recessive alleles; this reduces fertility and survival (inbreeding depression) and the population is less able to adapt to change or disease.
parts.working: 1 mark: low genetic diversity / small gene pool. 1 mark: inbreeding → more homozygous recessive harmful alleles expressed. 1 mark: reduced fitness/fertility or less able to adapt (e.g. to disease).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and embryo transfer could be used to produce offspring of a rare antelope, using a female of a common, closely related species as a surrogate mother.
parts.answer: Give the rare female hormones to stimulate many eggs to mature (superovulation); collect eggs (from ovaries); collect sperm from a rare male (or use frozen sperm); mix eggs and sperm in a dish (in vitro) for fertilisation; grow embryos for a few days in culture; implant embryo into the uterus of the surrogate female of the common species, whose cycle has been synchronised with hormones.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: hormones to stimulate egg production; eggs collected; sperm collected / thawed from frozen store; fertilisation in a dish/outside the body; embryos cultured; embryos implanted into surrogate; surrogate's cycle synchronised / prepared with hormones.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the advantages of using a surrogate of a common species and of keeping frozen embryos and sperm in a 'frozen zoo'.
parts.answer: Rare females are not put at risk by pregnancy and can produce more eggs/offspring; more offspring per year from each rare female; frozen material can be stored for many years and transported between countries instead of animals; genetic diversity is preserved and can be reintroduced into future populations, even from animals that have died.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: protects rare female / more offspring; many embryos per rare female; long-term storage; easy transport between zoos/countries; preserves genetic diversity for the future; use material from dead animals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how seeds are prepared and stored in a seed bank.
parts.answer: Seeds are cleaned and checked; dried to a low water content (about 5 %); sealed in airtight containers; stored at low temperature (about −20 °C); samples are germinated regularly to check viability, and new seed is grown when viability falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: dried to low water content; airtight containers; low temperature (e.g. −20 °C); germination tests at intervals; regrow to collect fresh seed; records kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many farmers in northern Pakistan have replaced old local wheat varieties with modern high-yielding varieties. Explain why seeds of the old local varieties are being collected and stored.
parts.answer: Old varieties contain alleles not found in modern varieties (genetic diversity); some may give resistance to diseases, drought, cold or salinity; these alleles could be bred into future crop varieties as the climate or pathogens change; once the varieties are no longer grown they may be lost for ever.
parts.working: 1 mark: preserves genetic diversity / alleles. 1 mark: useful traits (e.g. drought or disease resistance). 1 mark: for future breeding / prevent loss (extinction of variety).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the role of CITES in conservation.
parts.answer: CITES is an international agreement that regulates or bans international trade in endangered species and products made from them; species are listed in appendices according to how threatened they are (e.g. Appendix I – commercial trade banned; others need permits).
parts.working: 1 mark: international agreement controlling trade in endangered species / their products. 1 mark: species listed in appendices with different levels of restriction / permits needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one mountain area of Pakistan, a small number of permits to hunt old male markhor are sold each year to foreign hunters. Most of the money goes to the local community, which employs game guards. Suggest how this scheme can help the markhor population to increase.
parts.answer: Local people gain income from markhor, so they value live animals and stop poaching; game guards protect markhor from illegal hunting; only a few old males past their prime breeding age are taken, so the breeding population is hardly affected; money can also be used for habitat protection and community projects.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: income gives incentive to conserve; reduced poaching / guards employed; only few old males removed so breeding not affected; funds habitat protection; community support for conservation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The markhor's IUCN Red List category improved from Endangered to Near Threatened. State what the IUCN Red List is.
parts.answer: A list that assesses and classifies species according to their risk of extinction (e.g. Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable).
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Prosopis juliflora, a shrub from Central and South America, was introduced to Pakistan to provide fuel wood and to stabilise sand. It has since spread over large areas of grazing land and river banks in Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why Prosopis juliflora has been able to spread so rapidly in Sindh.
parts.answer: No natural predators, herbivores or diseases that control it in its new range; it tolerates drought and salty soils better than native plants; it produces many seeds that are spread by livestock eating the pods; it outcompetes native plants for water and light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: lack of natural predators/pathogens; tolerance of drought/salinity; large seed production; seeds dispersed by animals; outcompetes native species (deep roots for water, shading).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the spread of an invasive species such as P. juliflora can reduce biodiversity.
parts.answer: It outcompetes native plants, which decline or disappear locally; animals that depend on those plants for food or habitat also decline, so species diversity (and the variety of habitats) falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: native plants outcompeted / lost. 1 mark: knock-on loss of animals that depend on them / habitat becomes uniform.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two methods that could be used to control P. juliflora and give one disadvantage of one of them.
parts.answer: Mechanical removal (uprooting/cutting); herbicides; using the wood for fuel/charcoal to encourage harvesting; introducing a biological control agent (seed-eating insect) after testing; replanting native species. Disadvantage: e.g. herbicides may kill native plants or pollute water; cutting is labour-intensive and stumps resprout; a biological control agent might attack native species.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two methods. 1 mark for a valid disadvantage of one of them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the elephant population in a fenced reserve may need to be controlled.
parts.answer: With no natural predators and no way to migrate out of the reserve, the population grows beyond the carrying capacity; elephants destroy trees and vegetation, reducing habitat and food for other species (and for themselves), lowering biodiversity.
parts.working: 1 mark: population exceeds carrying capacity / no predators or migration. 1 mark: overgrazing / habitat damage reduces biodiversity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of culling and of contraception as methods of controlling the population.
parts.answer: Culling: reduces numbers quickly; meat/ivory/hide may provide income; but it is unpopular/ethically controversial, disturbs social groups and causes stress to remaining animals. Contraception (e.g. immunocontraceptive vaccine darted into females): humane and reversible, keeps social groups intact; but slow to reduce numbers (elephants are long-lived), must be repeated, expensive and needs each female to be identified and treated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four, with at least one advantage and one disadvantage for each method: culling fast / income vs ethical objection / social disruption; contraception humane / reversible / groups intact vs slow effect / repeated treatment / cost / labour.

practice.stem:
Forty captive-bred gazelles were released into a protected desert reserve in 2014. The population was counted every two years.
Year: 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024
Number: 40, 52, 71, 66, 94, 118

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in population from release (2014) to 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest reasons for the fall in numbers between 2018 and 2020.
parts.answer: Drought/reduced food or water; disease; predation; poaching; animals moving out of the reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: All 40 animals released came from one captive population. Discuss whether this reintroduction can be considered a long-term success.
parts.answer: Success: population has nearly tripled and is breeding in the wild. Concerns: all descended from 40 related animals, so genetic diversity is low – risk of inbreeding and less ability to adapt to disease or climate change; numbers fluctuate and the population is still small; long-term success needs continued monitoring, protection and perhaps introduction of unrelated animals.
parts.working: 1 mark: evidence of success (increase, breeding). 1 mark: low genetic diversity / founder effect / inbreeding risk. 1 mark: still small/fluctuating, needs further protection or new genetic stock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the taxonomic ranks in order from domain to species.
parts.answer: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
parts.working: 2 marks all in correct order; 1 mark with one error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tiger is Panthera tigris and the lion is Panthera leo. State the lowest taxonomic rank that both share and explain how you know.
parts.answer: Genus; both have the same first part of the binomial name (Panthera), which is the genus.
parts.working: 1 mark: genus. 1 mark: first name in binomial = genus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the domain and kingdom to which the tiger belongs.
parts.answer: Eukarya; Animalia.
parts.working: 1 mark (both needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table to compare the three domains.
Feature | Bacteria | Archaea | Eukarya
nucleus surrounded by envelope | ? | ? | ?
size of ribosomes in cytoplasm | ? | ? | ?
peptidoglycan in cell wall | ? | ? | ?
membrane lipids | ? | ? | ?
parts.answer:
nucleus: absent, absent, present
ribosomes: 70S, 70S, 80S
peptidoglycan: present, absent, absent
membrane lipids: unbranched fatty acids with ester bonds; branched chains with ether bonds; unbranched fatty acids with ester bonds
parts.working: 1 mark per correct row.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why organisms in the domain Archaea were once classified with bacteria.
parts.answer: They are prokaryotic: single cells with no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, similar in size and shape to bacteria.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature in which Archaea are more similar to Eukarya than to Bacteria.
parts.answer: Their RNA polymerase is more complex (similar to that of eukaryotes) / some have histone proteins associated with DNA / similar initiation of protein synthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
Descriptions of four eukaryotic organisms:
W: multicellular body made of thread-like hyphae; cell walls of chitin; feeds by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products; stores glycogen
X: single cell with chloroplasts and one flagellum; no cell wall; can also take in food when kept in the dark
Y: multicellular; cellulose cell walls; chloroplasts; stores starch
Z: multicellular; no cell walls; heterotrophic, ingests food; nervous coordination

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the kingdom to which each organism belongs.
parts.answer: W Fungi; X Protoctista; Y Plantae; Z Animalia.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why organism X is not placed in the plant kingdom, even though it has chloroplasts.
parts.answer: It is unicellular and has no cellulose cell wall; plants are multicellular with cellulose cell walls (and it can move by a flagellum and feed heterotrophically).
parts.working: 1 mark: unicellular (plants are multicellular). 1 mark: no cellulose cell wall / has flagellum.

practice.stem:
Information about the genetic material of four viruses:
Influenza virus: RNA, one strand, in eight segments
Smallpox (variola) virus: DNA, two complementary strands
T4 bacteriophage: DNA, two complementary strands
HIV: RNA, one strand (two identical copies per particle)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why viruses are not classified in any of the three domains.
parts.answer: Viruses are not cells (acellular: no cytoplasm, ribosomes or cell membrane); they cannot metabolise or reproduce outside a host cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: not made of cells / no ribosomes or cytoplasm. 1 mark: only replicate inside host cells / no metabolism.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the two features of the nucleic acid that are used to classify viruses.
parts.answer: Whether it is DNA or RNA; whether it is single-stranded or double-stranded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use these features to classify each virus.
parts.answer: Influenza virus: single-stranded RNA; smallpox virus: double-stranded DNA; T4 bacteriophage: double-stranded DNA; HIV: single-stranded RNA.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

practice.stem:
A segment of the gene for ribosomal RNA was sequenced in four organisms. The table shows the number of base differences between each pair of organisms in a 100-base region.
J–K: 31; J–L: 33; J–M: 6; K–L: 35; K–M: 30; L–M: 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, state which organism is most closely related to organism J and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Organism M; it has the fewest differences in its rRNA gene sequence from J (6), so they shared a common ancestor most recently.
parts.working: 1 mark: M. 1 mark: fewest base differences → most recent common ancestor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Organisms J and M are prokaryotes that live in hot, acidic springs. Organism K is a bacterium found in soil. Organism L is a yeast. Suggest which domain J and M belong to, giving a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Archaea; J and M differ from K (a bacterium) by about as many bases as from L (a eukaryote), so they are not closely related to bacteria even though they are prokaryotes.
parts.working: 1 mark: Archaea. 1 mark: as different from bacterium K as from eukaryote L (data quote: 31 and 33 differences).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why comparing sequences of genes such as ribosomal RNA genes led to the three-domain classification system.
parts.answer: rRNA genes are found in all organisms and change slowly by mutation; the number of differences reflects time since organisms shared a common ancestor; sequencing showed archaea were as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes, so three groups were needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: all organisms have the gene / differences accumulate over time (molecular clock). 1 mark: archaea shown to be distinct from bacteria, giving three domains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Biodiversity can be considered at three levels. Name and describe each level.
parts.answer: Ecosystem (habitat) diversity – the range of different ecosystems/habitats in an area; species diversity – the number of different species and the evenness of their abundance (species richness and relative abundance); genetic diversity – the variety of alleles within a species/population.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ecosystem/habitat diversity; species diversity (number and relative abundance of species); genetic diversity (variation of alleles within species).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a student could place quadrats randomly in a grassland, and explain why random sampling is used.
parts.answer: Lay two tapes at right angles along two sides of the area to form axes; use a random number generator to select pairs of coordinates; place the quadrat at each coordinate. Random sampling avoids bias in choosing where to sample, so the samples are representative of the whole area.
parts.working: 1 mark: grid / tapes as axes. 1 mark: random number generator / table for coordinates. 1 mark: avoids bias, representative samples (allows statistical testing).

practice.stem: Pitfall traps were set in a cotton field near Multan. 60 ground beetles were caught, marked with a dot of non-toxic paint on the underside and released. Two days later 75 beetles were caught, of which 12 were marked.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the estimated population size of ground beetles using the Lincoln index.
parts.answer: 375 beetles

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three assumptions that must be true for this estimate to be valid.
parts.answer: Marked beetles mix randomly with the rest of the population; marks do not rub off; marking does not affect survival or behaviour (e.g. make beetles more visible to predators); no significant births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples; all beetles equally likely to be caught.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem:
A student counted the plants of each species in quadrats in two areas of the Margalla Hills: site A, natural forest edge, and site B, a pine plantation.
Site A (species 1–6): 18, 12, 9, 7, 3, 1
Site B (species 1–4): 38, 6, 4, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Simpson's index of diversity (D = 1 − Σ(n/N)²) for each site. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Site A: D = 0.76; site B: D = 0.40

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the biodiversity of the two sites and suggest a reason for the difference.
parts.answer: Site A (natural forest) has higher diversity: more species and more even numbers; site B is dominated by one species. The plantation has one tree species, so fewer niches/habitats and food sources; management (clearing undergrowth) removes other plants.
parts.working: 1 mark: A higher diversity – more species and more even abundance (B dominated by species 1). 1 mark: plantation = single tree species / fewer niches / management.

practice.stem:
An ecologist recorded the percentage tree cover and the number of bird species at eight sites around Islamabad.
Site: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Tree cover / %: 12, 25, 38, 47, 55, 63, 71, 84
Bird species: 9, 14, 12, 19, 17, 24, 28, 26

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between percentage tree cover and the number of bird species.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, rs = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)). Show your working. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1: ranks – tree cover 1–8 in order; bird species ranks 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 8, 7. M1: Σd² = 6. A1: 1 − 36 ÷ 504 = 0.93.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.738. Explain what your result shows.
parts.answer: 0.93 is greater than 0.738, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant positive correlation between tree cover and the number of bird species (more tree cover, more bird species).
parts.working: 1 mark: rs > critical value, reject null. 1 mark: significant positive correlation (not chance at p < 0.05).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a high tree cover is associated with more bird species.
parts.answer: More trees provide more niches – nesting sites, shelter and food sources (insects, fruit) for different species.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A student placed 10 quadrats, each 0.5 m × 0.5 m (0.25 m²), at random on a school playing field of area 1200 m² and counted the dandelion plants in each.
Numbers: 3, 5, 2, 0, 4, 6, 1, 3, 2, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of dandelion plants per quadrat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean density of dandelions per m².
parts.answer: 12 per m²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the total number of dandelions on the field.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why this estimate may not be accurate.
parts.answer: Only 10 quadrats sampled (small sample); dandelions may be clumped/unevenly distributed; counting errors at quadrat edges.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one valid reason.

practice.stem:
A survey estimated the number of mature individuals of a vulture species in a region at 3400 in 2014 and 1450 in 2024.
One criterion used by the IUCN states that a population reduction over 10 years of at least 80 % qualifies a species as Critically Endangered, at least 50 % as Endangered and at least 30 % as Vulnerable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the population between 2014 and 2024. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the criterion given to state the category the species qualifies for, and explain your choice.
parts.answer: Endangered, because the decline (57.4 %) is at least 50 % but less than 80 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: Endangered with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean decrease in number of individuals per year.
parts.answer: 195 individuals per year

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a survey of mature individuals, rather than all individuals, is used to judge extinction risk.
parts.answer: Only mature individuals can breed and produce the next generation, so their number determines whether the population can recover.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Students compared seaweed cover on two rocky shores near Karachi. On each shore they chose five places that looked typical, placed a 1 m² quadrat at each and estimated by eye the percentage cover of each seaweed species. One shore was sampled at low tide on a morning, the other in the afternoon a week later when the tide was coming in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three limitations of this method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Percentage cover estimated by eye is subjective – use a quadrat divided into 100 small squares/point quadrat, and the same person to estimate. Quadrats placed where the student chose – use random coordinates (or regular intervals along a belt transect). Only 5 quadrats – sample more (e.g. 20) until the running mean levels off. Some species may be misidentified – use an identification key/photograph. Samples taken at different states of the tide or on different days – sample at the same time on the same day.
parts.working: 1 mark per limitation and 1 mark per matching improvement, for three pairs (max 6).

practice.stem:
Students used mark–release–recapture to estimate the number of land snails in a garden. They noted three problems:
1: water-based paint used to mark the shells washed off in rain
2: bright paint was put on the top of the shell, where birds could see it
3: the second sample was taken 20 minutes after release, close to the release point

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each problem, explain how it would affect the population estimate (too high or too low).
parts.answer: 1: marked snails in the second sample are fewer than they should be, so the estimate is too high. 2: if marked snails are eaten more, fewer marked are recaptured, so the estimate is too high. 3: marked snails have not mixed, so recapturing near the release point gives too many marked snails (estimate too low) – or too few if sampling elsewhere (too high).
parts.working: 1 mark each: (1) too high; (2) too high; (3) explained either way – not randomly mixed, so ratio not representative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement for each problem.
parts.answer: 1: use waterproof, non-toxic paint/permanent marker and check it does not rub off in a trial. 2: mark on the underside or in an inconspicuous place / use a dull colour. 3: leave a longer time (e.g. 24 h) for mixing and sample from the whole area.
parts.working: 1 mark per improvement.

practice.stem:
Belt transects were used to sample butterflies at six urban and six rural sites near Lahore. Simpson's index of diversity was calculated for each site.
Urban: mean D = 0.62, 95 % confidence interval ± 0.07
Rural: mean D = 0.81, 95 % confidence interval ± 0.05

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that butterfly diversity is higher in rural sites than in urban sites. Use the data to evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Mean D is higher in rural sites (0.81 vs 0.62). The 95 % confidence intervals (rural 0.76–0.86, urban 0.55–0.69) do not overlap, so the difference is significant and the conclusion is supported for these sites. But only 6 sites of each type, sampled in one season/year, in one city, so it may not apply generally.
parts.working: 1 mark: rural higher with data. 1 mark: CIs do not overlap so significant. 1 mark: limitation – few sites / one season / one region.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why butterfly diversity is lower in urban areas.
parts.answer: Fewer flowering plants/nectar sources and larval food plants; habitat loss and fragmentation by buildings and roads; pollution/pesticide use; higher temperature/light at night.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Lichen diversity on tree trunks was recorded at seven distances (5 m to 200 m) from a busy road. Spearman's rank correlation between distance from the road and lichen diversity gave rs = 0.86. The critical value for n = 7 at p = 0.05 is 0.79.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concluded that pollution from vehicles on the road causes the decrease in lichen diversity. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: The significant positive correlation shows lichen diversity increases with distance from the road (rs = 0.86 > 0.79), which is consistent with pollution from traffic. However, correlation does not prove causation; other variables also change with distance, e.g. dust, light, humidity, trampling, tree species or bark pH; pollution was not measured; only one road and 7 points, so the conclusion is tentative.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation significant and positive, supports link. 1 mark: correlation ≠ causation. 1 mark: named confounding variable(s) changing with distance. 1 mark: pollution not measured / small sample / one road.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one further measurement that would test whether vehicle pollution is the cause.
parts.answer: Measure the concentration of nitrogen dioxide/sulfur dioxide (or particulates) in the air at each distance and correlate with lichen diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the species richness of plants in a grazed area and an ungrazed (fenced) area of hillside.
parts.answer: Choose two areas of similar slope, aspect and soil; mark out each with tapes as axes; use random number coordinates to place 1 m² (or 0.25 m²) quadrats; use at least 20 quadrats in each area (or until a running mean levels off); count the number of different plant species in each quadrat, using an identification key; also record abundance/percentage cover if Simpson's index is to be calculated; sample both areas at the same time of year; calculate mean species per quadrat and compare with a t-test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: areas matched for other variables (slope, aspect, soil); random sampling method with coordinates; quadrat size stated; sufficient number of quadrats (≥10, ideally 20+); DV species per quadrat identified with key; same time/season; abundance recorded for Simpson's index; means calculated; t-test to compare.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field investigation into how the abundance of a fern changes with light intensity from the inside of a woodland into an open field.
parts.answer: Lay a tape from inside the wood, across the edge and into the field; place quadrats at regular intervals (e.g. every 2 m) along the tape – a belt or interrupted belt transect; in each quadrat record the abundance of the fern as percentage cover or number of fronds; measure light intensity at ground level in each quadrat with a light meter, at the same height and at the same time of day (or several readings averaged); repeat with two or three more transects at random positions along the wood edge; also record soil moisture/temperature as other variables; plot abundance against light intensity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: transect line across the edge; quadrats at regular intervals (belt/interrupted belt); abundance measure (% cover, count); light meter readings at each quadrat; same time of day / weather / height of meter; repeat transects; record other variables (soil moisture, pH, temperature); at least 10 sampling points; plot scatter graph of abundance against light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the statistical test that should be used to analyse the results and explain your choice.
parts.answer: Spearman's rank correlation – to test for a correlation between two variables (light intensity and abundance) whose data may not be normally distributed.
parts.working: 1 mark: Spearman's rank with reason (testing correlation between two variables).

practice.stem: A student wants to find out whether the number of mayfly larvae in streams flowing into Rawal Lake is related to the concentration of dissolved oxygen in the water. She will use a kick-sampling net for 1 minute at each site and measure dissolved oxygen with a meter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: dissolved oxygen concentration (site). Dependent: number (abundance) of mayfly larvae.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a field study the other variables cannot be controlled. Name three variables that might affect the number of mayfly larvae and describe how the student could take account of them.
parts.answer: Any three: water temperature; flow rate; type of stream bed (stones vs mud); depth; pH; shading. Choose sites that are similar in these variables (e.g. same depth and stone size), and measure them at each site (thermometer, flow meter, pH probe) so that their effects can be considered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three variables (max 3). 1 mark for: choose similar sites or measure and record them to take into account.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A wetland plant was counted in four zones of equal area around a pond. The total was 120 plants.
Zone 1: 28; zone 2: 41; zone 3: 19; zone 4: 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: The plants are distributed evenly (randomly) across the four zones; any difference from the expected numbers is due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of χ², using χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value at p = 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom is 7.82. Explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: 8.33 > 7.82, so reject the null hypothesis; the difference between observed and expected numbers is significant – the plants are not evenly distributed (more in zone 2, fewer in zone 3).
parts.working: 1 mark: χ² greater than critical value, reject null. 1 mark: distribution significantly different from even / not due to chance.

practice.stem: Students will collect invertebrates by kick-sampling in a shallow, fast-flowing stream in the hills and measure the water temperature and flow rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three hazards of this fieldwork and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Slipping or falling into the stream/drowning – work in pairs, wear boots with grip, stay in shallow water, check water level and weather. Infection from contaminated water (e.g. bacteria from animal urine or sewage) – wear gloves, cover cuts, wash hands. Sunburn/heat stroke – hat, sunscreen, drinking water. Insect or snake bites – long sleeves, look before placing hands. Getting lost – tell someone the route and return time.
parts.working: 1 mark for each hazard with a matching precaution (max 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the overall level of risk and give a reason.
parts.answer: Medium – working in or near flowing water has a risk of serious harm, although it can be reduced by the precautions.
parts.working: 1 mark: level with justification (accept low with good justification of shallow water and supervision).

practice.stem: An ecologist plans to measure Simpson's index of diversity of plants in quadrats at 100 m intervals from 100 m to 1000 m from a cement factory, where dust from the factory settles on the vegetation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a testable hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Species diversity of plants increases as distance from the cement factory increases.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between distance from the factory and plant species diversity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the results and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Diversity will be lowest near the factory and increase with distance, because dust settling on leaves near the factory blocks light and stomata (and changes soil pH), so only a few tolerant species survive there.
parts.working: 1 mark: prediction (diversity increases with distance). 1 mark: explanation (dust reduces photosynthesis / alters soil pH; only tolerant species survive).

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In a species of flowering plant grown in a research garden in Faisalabad, the allele for purple flowers, F, is dominant to the allele for white flowers, f.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the terms 'dominant' and 'homozygous'.
parts.answer: Dominant: an allele that is expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote (whenever it is present). Homozygous: having two identical alleles of a gene (at the same locus on a pair of homologous chromosomes).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A purple-flowered plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a white-flowered plant. Use genetic diagrams to show how the offspring would show the genotype of the purple-flowered plant.
parts.answer: Test cross with ff. If FF × ff: gametes F and f; all offspring Ff, purple. If Ff × ff: gametes F, f and f; offspring Ff : ff = 1 purple : 1 white. Any white offspring shows the parent is Ff; all purple (in a large sample) suggests FF.
parts.working: B1 key to alleles and parental genotypes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring genotypes and phenotypes for both crosses; B1 conclusion linking ratio to genotype.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: The ABO blood group gene has three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant and both are dominant to Iᴼ. In a family in Peshawar, the father has blood group A and the mother has blood group B. Their first child has blood group O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the genotypes of the father and the mother. Explain how you know.
parts.answer: Father IᴬIᴼ; mother IᴮIᴼ; the group O child is IᴼIᴼ, so must have received an Iᴼ from each parent.
parts.working: B1 both genotypes; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible blood groups of their children and state the probability that their next child has blood group AB.
parts.answer: Gametes: Iᴬ, Iᴼ and Iᴮ, Iᴼ. Offspring: IᴬIᴮ (AB), IᴬIᴼ (A), IᴮIᴼ (B), IᴼIᴼ (O) in 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Probability AB = 1/4 (0.25).
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 four genotypes with phenotypes; B1 1/4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why blood group AB shows codominance.
parts.answer: Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote: both antigen A and antigen B are present on the red cells.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In shorthorn cattle, the allele Cᴿ gives red hair and the allele Cᵂ gives white hair. Heterozygous cattle, CᴿCᵂ, are roan: they have a mixture of red hairs and white hairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is an example of codominance.
parts.answer: Both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote – red and white hairs are both present.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A farmer crossed roan bulls with roan cows and 24 calves were born. Draw a genetic diagram and state the expected numbers of red, roan and white calves.
parts.answer: Gametes Cᴿ, Cᵂ from each parent; offspring CᴿCᴿ red : CᴿCᵂ roan : CᵂCᵂ white = 1 : 2 : 1; expected 6 red, 12 roan, 6 white.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes/1 : 2 : 1; A1 6, 12, 6.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Haemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele, Xʰ, of a gene on the X chromosome. A woman whose father had haemophilia marries a man without haemophilia. Neither of them has haemophilia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the genotypes of the woman and the man.
parts.answer: Woman XᴴXʰ (carrier – she inherited Xʰ from her father); man XᴴY.
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible genotypes and phenotypes of their children.
parts.answer: Gametes: Xᴴ, Xʰ (mother); Xᴴ, Y (father). Children: XᴴXᴴ unaffected female; XᴴXʰ carrier female; XᴴY unaffected male; XʰY male with haemophilia.
parts.working: B1 gametes including Y; B1 four genotypes; B1 phenotypes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate (i) the probability that a son of this couple has haemophilia, and (ii) the probability that any child of this couple will be a son with haemophilia.
parts.working: B1 1/2 (half of sons); B1 1/4 (one of four equally likely children).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why haemophilia is much more common in males than in females.
parts.answer: Males have only one X chromosome, so one recessive allele causes the condition (no second allele to mask it); females need two copies.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In a species of tomato, red fruit (R) is dominant to yellow fruit (r) and tall stem (T) is dominant to dwarf stem (t). The two genes are on different chromosomes. Two plants heterozygous for both genes were crossed and 320 offspring were produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the genotypes of the gametes that each parent can produce, and explain why there are four types.
parts.answer: RT, Rt, rT, rt; the genes are on different chromosomes, so they assort independently in meiosis (metaphase I/anaphase I), giving four combinations in equal numbers.
parts.working: B1 four gametes; B1 independent assortment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers of each phenotype among the 320 offspring.
parts.answer: red tall 180; red dwarf 60; yellow tall 60; yellow dwarf 20
parts.working: M1 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio; M1 320 ÷ 16 = 20 per sixteenth; A1 all four numbers.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In summer squash, fruit colour is controlled by two genes on different chromosomes. A dominant allele W prevents any pigment forming, so the fruit is white. In ww plants, allele Y (dominant) gives yellow fruit and yy gives green fruit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the phenotypes of plants with genotypes WwYy, wwYy and wwyy.
parts.answer: WwYy white; wwYy yellow; wwyy green.
parts.working: B1 all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two WwYy plants are crossed and 160 plants are grown from the seeds. Calculate the expected number of white, yellow and green plants. Show your reasoning.
parts.answer: white 120; yellow 30; green 10

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this cross differs from the 9 : 3 : 4 ratio seen in Labrador coat colour.
parts.answer: Here the epistatic allele is dominant (one W masks the other gene), giving 12 : 3 : 1; in Labradors the epistatic allele is recessive (ee needed to mask), giving 9 : 3 : 4.
parts.working: B1 dominant vs recessive epistasis; B1 ratios linked.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Coat colour in rabbits is controlled by one gene with four alleles. In order of dominance: C (full colour) > cᶜʰ (chinchilla, silver-grey) > cʰ (Himalayan, white with dark extremities) > c (albino).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chinchilla rabbit with genotype cᶜʰc is crossed with a Himalayan rabbit with genotype cʰc. Draw a genetic diagram to show the expected genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring, and state the phenotypic ratio.
parts.answer: Gametes cᶜʰ, c and cʰ, c. Offspring: cᶜʰcʰ chinchilla; cᶜʰc chinchilla; cʰc Himalayan; cc albino. Ratio 2 chinchilla : 1 Himalayan : 1 albino.
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 four genotypes; B1 phenotypes; A1 ratio 2 : 1 : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of different genotypes possible for this gene in the rabbit population.
parts.working: B1 4 homozygotes + 6 heterozygotes = 10.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In domestic cats, a gene on the X chromosome controls orange or black fur. Xᴼ gives orange fur and Xᴮ gives black fur. The alleles are codominant: a female XᴼXᴮ is tortoiseshell (patches of orange and black).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tortoiseshell female is mated with a black male. Draw a genetic diagram to show the phenotypes of the kittens and their sexes.
parts.answer: XᴼXᴮ × XᴮY; gametes Xᴼ, Xᴮ and Xᴮ, Y; kittens: XᴼXᴮ tortoiseshell female; XᴮXᴮ black female; XᴼY orange male; XᴮY black male.
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes and gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes with sexes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the probability that a kitten from this cross is tortoiseshell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why tortoiseshell cats are almost always female.
parts.answer: Tortoiseshell needs both Xᴼ and Xᴮ, so two X chromosomes are needed; males (XY) have only one X chromosome so can be only orange or black (rare XXY males can be tortoiseshell).
parts.working: B1 needs two X chromosomes/both alleles; B1 males XY have one X.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In a cereal plant, the allele for coloured grain (C) is dominant to colourless grain (c), and the allele for smooth grain (S) is dominant to wrinkled grain (s). A plant heterozygous for both genes, CcSs, which had received C and S from one parent and c and s from the other, was crossed with a plant with colourless, wrinkled grains. Offspring: coloured smooth 86; colourless wrinkled 82; coloured wrinkled 17; colourless smooth 15.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the ratio of phenotypes expected if the two genes assorted independently.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the results differ from this ratio.
parts.answer: The genes are linked – on the same chromosome (close together); C and S, and c and s, tend to be inherited together, so parental phenotypes (coloured smooth, colourless wrinkled) are most common; the small numbers of coloured wrinkled and colourless smooth are recombinants produced by crossing over between the loci in prophase I.
parts.working: B1 linkage/same chromosome; B1 parental combinations inherited together; B1 recombinants from crossing over (chiasmata).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of offspring that are recombinants.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: Coat colour in Labrador retriever dogs is controlled by two genes on different chromosomes. Gene B/b: B gives black pigment, b gives chocolate (brown) pigment. Gene E/e: at least one E allele allows pigment to be deposited in the hair; ee dogs are yellow whatever their B/b alleles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name this type of gene interaction and explain why.
parts.answer: Epistasis (recessive epistasis); the homozygous recessive ee genotype at one locus masks the expression of the B/b gene at another locus.
parts.working: B1 epistasis; B1 ee masks/prevents expression of B/b.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two black dogs, both BbEe, are mated many times. Use a genetic diagram to show the expected phenotypic ratio of their puppies.
parts.answer: Gametes: BE, Be, bE, be from each parent. 16 combinations: B_E_ 9 black; bbE_ 3 chocolate; B_ee 3 yellow and bbee 1 yellow, so 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow.
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 Punnett square/16 genotypes; B1 genotypes linked to phenotypes; A1 9 : 3 : 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Over several litters the dogs had 64 puppies. Calculate the expected number of yellow puppies.

practice.subtopic: Genetic crosses (mono/dihybrid, sex linkage, codominance, epistasis)
practice.stem: In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, white eyes are caused by a recessive allele, Xʷ, on the X chromosome (red eyes Xᵂ). Vestigial wings are caused by a recessive allele, v, of a gene on an autosome (normal wings V). A red-eyed female with normal wings, genotype XᵂXʷ Vv, is crossed with a white-eyed male with normal wings, genotype XʷY Vv.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the probability that an offspring fly will be white-eyed with vestigial wings. Show your working.
parts.working: M1 P(white eyes) = 1/2 (XʷXʷ or XʷY from XᵂXʷ × XʷY); M1 P(vv) = 1/4; A1 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 400 offspring were counted. Calculate the expected number of white-eyed flies with vestigial wings, and the expected number of these that are female.
parts.answer: 50 white-eyed vestigial; 25 of them female
parts.working: B1 400 × 1/8 = 50; B1 half are XʷXʷ females = 25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a male fly cannot pass the Xʷ allele to his sons.
parts.answer: Sons receive the Y chromosome from their father (and their X from the mother).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The lac operon of Escherichia coli contains a promoter, an operator and three structural genes. State what is meant by a structural gene and a regulatory gene.
parts.answer: Structural gene: codes for a protein (e.g. an enzyme) that has a function in the cell other than controlling other genes. Regulatory gene: codes for a protein (e.g. a repressor or transcription factor) that controls the expression of other genes.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the lac operon is kept switched off when lactose is absent.
parts.answer: The regulatory gene (lacI) is transcribed and translated to make the repressor protein; the repressor binds to the operator; this prevents RNA polymerase from binding to the promoter/moving along, so the structural genes are not transcribed.
parts.working: B1 repressor made by regulatory gene; B1 binds operator; B1 RNA polymerase blocked, no transcription of structural genes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the enzyme encoded by lacZ.
parts.answer: β-galactosidase

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a transcription factor in a eukaryotic cell.
parts.answer: A protein that binds to DNA (at a specific base sequence, e.g. a promoter) and controls whether a gene is transcribed; by increasing or decreasing the binding of RNA polymerase.
parts.working: B1 protein binding to DNA/promoter; B1 switches transcription on or off/helps or blocks RNA polymerase.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why different cell types in the same plant, such as guard cells and root hair cells, make different proteins although they contain the same genes.
parts.answer: Different transcription factors are active in different cell types, so different genes are switched on (transcribed) and others are switched off.
parts.working: B1 same genes but different genes expressed; B1 due to different transcription factors (or signals) in each cell type.

practice.stem: Mutant strains of E. coli were grown in a medium with no lactose and then in a medium with lactose. The amount of β-galactosidase was measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Strain 1 has a mutation in the regulatory gene so that the repressor protein cannot bind to the operator. Predict and explain the amount of β-galactosidase made in each medium.
parts.answer: Large amount in both media (made all the time/constitutive); the repressor cannot bind the operator, so RNA polymerase can always bind to the promoter and transcribe lacZ, even without lactose.
parts.working: B1 high in both; B1 repressor cannot block operator; B1 RNA polymerase transcribes structural genes continuously.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Strain 2 has a mutation in the regulatory gene so that the repressor still binds to the operator but cannot bind lactose (allolactose). Predict and explain the amount of β-galactosidase made in each medium.
parts.answer: Little or none in both media; normally lactose binds the repressor and changes its shape so it leaves the operator; this repressor cannot bind lactose, so it stays on the operator and the genes are never transcribed.
parts.working: B1 none/very low in both; B1 lactose normally changes repressor shape; B1 repressor stays bound, no transcription.

practice.stem: When a barley grain absorbs water, the embryo releases gibberellin (GA). GA causes cells of the aleurone layer to make amylase, which hydrolyses starch in the endosperm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how gibberellin causes the gene for amylase to be transcribed in an aleurone cell.
parts.answer: GA binds to a receptor protein (GID1) in the cell; the GA–receptor complex binds to DELLA proteins; this causes DELLA to be broken down (ubiquitination and destruction by proteasomes); DELLA normally binds to and inhibits a transcription factor (PIF); the freed transcription factor binds to the promoter of the amylase gene and RNA polymerase transcribes it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the production of amylase is important for germination.
parts.answer: Amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose/glucose; the sugars are respired by the embryo to release energy (ATP) for growth, and used to build new cells (cellulose).
parts.working: B1 starch → maltose/glucose; B1 for respiration/growth of embryo.

practice.stem: A bacterium makes the amino acid tryptophan using five enzymes coded by genes in one operon. When tryptophan was added to the growth medium, the concentration of these enzymes fell to almost zero within 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the tryptophan-synthesising enzymes are repressible or inducible, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Repressible; their synthesis is switched off (repressed) when the end product, tryptophan, is present.
parts.working: B1 repressible; B1 reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how tryptophan could switch off transcription of this operon.
parts.answer: Tryptophan binds to an (inactive) repressor protein, changing its shape so it can bind to the operator; this blocks RNA polymerase so the genes are not transcribed.
parts.working: B1 tryptophan binds repressor and activates it; B1 repressor binds operator, blocks transcription.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the advantage to the bacterium of controlling these genes in this way.
parts.answer: The bacterium does not waste energy, ATP and amino acids making enzymes (and tryptophan) when tryptophan is already available.
parts.working: B1 saves energy/resources; B1 only made when needed.

practice.stem: In eukaryotes, genes are not organised into operons. Each gene has its own promoter, and transcription starts only when the correct transcription factors and RNA polymerase have bound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the three structural genes of the lac operon are always transcribed together, while three genes coding for enzymes of one pathway in a eukaryote may be switched on separately.
parts.answer: In the lac operon the three genes share one promoter and operator and are transcribed as one mRNA; in eukaryotes each gene has its own promoter, so each can be controlled by its own transcription factors.
parts.working: B1 shared promoter/operator, one mRNA; B1 separate promoters/separate transcription factors in eukaryotes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mutation changes the base sequence of the promoter of a eukaryotic gene so that a transcription factor that activates the gene can no longer bind. Suggest the effect on the cell.
parts.answer: RNA polymerase does not bind/transcription is not started, so no (or little) mRNA and protein is made from that gene; the cell lacks the protein, e.g. an enzyme, so its function is lost.
parts.working: B1 no transcription/RNA polymerase not recruited; B1 protein not made and consequence.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which a transcription factor may be activated in response to a signal reaching a cell.
parts.answer: A hormone/signal binds a receptor, which leads to the transcription factor being changed (e.g. phosphorylated) or released from an inhibitor (as when GA causes DELLA breakdown).

practice.stem: A culture of E. coli growing without lactose was transferred at time 0 to a medium containing lactose and no glucose. β-galactosidase activity (arbitrary units): 0 min – 2; 2 min – 2; 5 min – 15; 10 min – 50; 20 min – 120; 30 min – 190.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in β-galactosidase activity between 10 and 20 minutes, in arbitrary units per minute.
parts.answer: 7 units min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the increase in β-galactosidase activity after lactose was added.
parts.answer: Lactose (allolactose) enters and binds to the repressor; the repressor changes shape and can no longer bind to the operator; RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and transcribes lacZ, lacY and lacA (one mRNA); mRNA is translated into β-galactosidase (and lactose permease, which lets more lactose in, so activity rises faster).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: lactose binds repressor; shape change, released from operator; RNA polymerase binds promoter; transcription of structural genes; translation; permease increases uptake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why there was no increase in activity in the first two minutes.
parts.answer: Time is needed for lactose to enter, for the repressor to be released and for transcription and translation to make new enzyme.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why β-galactosidase is described as an inducible enzyme.
parts.answer: It is made only when its substrate (lactose, the inducer) is present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Semi-dwarf wheat varieties grown widely in Pakistan since the 1960s carry mutant alleles of the Rht genes, which code for DELLA proteins. The mutant DELLA proteins are not broken down when gibberellin binds to its receptor. Explain why these plants have short stems even though they make normal amounts of gibberellin.
parts.answer: The mutant DELLA is not degraded, so it remains bound to the transcription factors (PIFs); genes that promote stem elongation/cell division are not transcribed; so stems grow less in response to GA (GA-insensitive).
parts.working: B1 DELLA not degraded; B1 continues to inhibit transcription factors; B1 growth genes not transcribed/GA has no effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In peas, tall plants have the dominant allele Le, which codes for an enzyme that converts an inactive gibberellin into active GA₁. The recessive allele le has a single base substitution. Suggest why lele plants are short.
parts.answer: The substitution changes one amino acid in the enzyme; the enzyme's tertiary structure/active site is altered so it has (much) lower activity; less active GA₁ is made, so DELLA proteins are not broken down and stem elongation is reduced.
parts.working: B1 amino acid changed; B1 enzyme less active/active site shape changed; B1 less GA₁, DELLA remains, less elongation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage to farmers of growing semi-dwarf wheat.
parts.answer: Short, strong stems are less likely to fall over (lodge) in wind/rain when carrying heavy heads of grain; more energy goes into grain, increasing yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a homologous pair of chromosomes.
parts.answer: Two chromosomes, one from each parent (maternal and paternal), that have the same genes at the same loci and are the same size and shape (centromere position); they may carry different alleles.
parts.working: B1 same genes at same loci; B1 one maternal and one paternal (may have different alleles).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the stage of meiosis in which (i) crossing over occurs and (ii) homologous chromosomes are separated.
parts.answer: (i) prophase I; (ii) anaphase I
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways in which the cells produced by meiosis differ from those produced by mitosis.
parts.answer: Meiosis gives haploid cells (half the chromosome number); four cells rather than two; cells genetically different from each other and from the parent cell.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how independent assortment in meiosis produces genetic variation among gametes.
parts.answer: At metaphase I each homologous pair lines up on the equator independently/randomly of other pairs; so the maternal and paternal chromosomes are shuffled into different combinations in each gamete.
parts.working: B1 random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I; B1 different combinations of maternal/paternal chromosomes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A plant species has a diploid number of 14. Calculate the number of genetically different gametes one plant could produce by independent assortment alone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of different chromosome combinations possible in a zygote produced from two plants of this species, by independent assortment and random fertilisation (ignore crossing over).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the real number of genetically different gametes is far larger than your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Crossing over in prophase I exchanges sections between non-sister chromatids, producing new combinations of alleles on each chromosome.

practice.stem: A student examined squashed anther cells of an onion (2n = 16) undergoing meiosis. Cell P: pairs of homologous chromosomes (bivalents) lined up across the middle of the cell. Cell Q: two groups of chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, moving to opposite poles. Cell R: four groups of single chromatids, in two cells, being pulled to the poles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the stage of meiosis shown in each cell.
parts.answer: P metaphase I; Q anaphase I; R anaphase II
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of chromosomes that will be present in each nucleus at the end of meiosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the separation of chromatids in meiosis II also contributes to genetic variation.
parts.answer: Because of crossing over, the sister chromatids of a chromosome are no longer identical; independent assortment of chromatids at metaphase II produces further new combinations in the four cells.
parts.working: B1 chromatids not identical after crossing over; B1 random arrangement at metaphase II.

practice.stem: The mass of DNA in a nucleus of a cell from the testis of a mammal was measured during one meiotic division. Mass in arbitrary units: before the S phase (G1) – 20; end of interphase – 40; after telophase I – 20; after telophase II – 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the changes in mass of DNA shown by these data.
parts.answer: 20 → 40: DNA replicates in S phase of interphase, each chromosome now two chromatids; 40 → 20: at the end of meiosis I homologous chromosomes separate into two nuclei, so each nucleus gets half the DNA (still two chromatids per chromosome); 20 → 10: in meiosis II sister chromatids separate, giving haploid nuclei with half the DNA of the original G1 cell.
parts.working: B1 replication in S phase; B1 homologues separate in meiosis I; B1 chromatids separate in meiosis II; B1 final nuclei haploid with half the original DNA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sperm cell fertilises an egg. State the DNA mass, in arbitrary units, of the zygote nucleus before it replicates, and explain the significance of this for the species.
parts.answer: 20; the diploid chromosome number (and DNA content) is restored at fertilisation, so it stays constant from generation to generation.
parts.working: B1 20; B1 diploid number restored/maintained between generations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how meiosis and fertilisation together produce genetic variation in the offspring of sexually reproducing organisms.
parts.answer: Points: in prophase I homologous chromosomes pair (bivalents); non-sister chromatids form chiasmata and exchange sections (crossing over); this produces new combinations of alleles on chromatids; at metaphase I homologous pairs line up randomly/independent assortment; giving 2ⁿ combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes; at metaphase II chromatids (no longer identical) assort independently; random fertilisation – any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete; mating between unrelated individuals combines different alleles; gametes haploid so zygote combines alleles from two parents.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six points; max 4 if fertilisation is not mentioned.

practice.stem:
A dihybrid cross between two plants heterozygous for flower colour and leaf shape was expected to give a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. Observed offspring: 93, 29, 31 and 7 (total 160).
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. Critical values at p = 0.05: 1 df – 3.84; 2 df – 5.99; 3 df – 7.82.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers for each class.
parts.working: B1 all four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom and explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: 3 degrees of freedom (4 classes − 1); 1.07 < 7.82, so the difference between observed and expected is not significant (p > 0.05); it is due to chance, and the results fit a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: B1 3 df; B1 not significant, accept null/fits ratio.

practice.stem:
A breeder in Karachi mated BbEe Labrador dogs (B black, b chocolate; ee dogs are yellow whatever their B/b alleles) and recorded 160 puppies over several years: 98 black, 22 chocolate, 40 yellow. The expected ratio is 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow.
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. Critical values at p = 0.05: 1 df – 3.84; 2 df – 5.99; 3 df – 7.82.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the observed numbers and the numbers expected from a 9 : 3 : 4 ratio (any difference is due to chance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ². Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State a conclusion, using the critical values.
parts.answer: 2 degrees of freedom; 2.84 < 5.99, so accept the null hypothesis: the difference is not significant and the results are consistent with recessive epistasis (9 : 3 : 4).
parts.working: B1 2 df and comparison; B1 not significant/consistent with 9 : 3 : 4.

practice.stem: A geneticist has two true-breeding stocks of Drosophila: one with normal (red) eyes and one with a new mutant eye colour, 'sepia-like'. She wants to find out whether the mutant allele is recessive, and whether the gene is on the X chromosome or on an autosome.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how she could carry out breeding experiments to answer these questions. Include the crosses, how the flies are handled, and the results she would expect for each possibility.
parts.answer: Points: collect virgin females (isolate within about 8 h of emerging) so the female parents have not mated; reciprocal crosses – mutant female × normal male and normal female × mutant male; anaesthetise flies (e.g. CO₂) to sex and score them; keep cultures at a constant temperature (e.g. 25 °C) on the same medium; remove parents before offspring emerge; if all F1 in both crosses are normal, mutant is recessive; if reciprocal crosses give the same results (all F1 normal), gene is autosomal; if mutant female × normal male gives normal females but all mutant males, the gene is X-linked; interbreed F1 to get F2 and score phenotypes by sex – autosomal recessive gives 3 : 1 in both sexes; use large numbers and test fit with χ².
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven points; must include reciprocal crosses and the expected results for at least one possibility for full marks.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student counted the kernels on one ear of maize produced by a test cross between a plant heterozygous for purple kernels (Pp) and a plant with yellow kernels (pp). There were 212 purple and 188 yellow kernels.
χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. Critical value at p = 0.05 for 1 df is 3.84.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a χ² test, not a t-test, is the appropriate statistical test for these data.
parts.answer: The data are counts in categories (frequencies of discrete phenotypes), compared with expected numbers from a predicted ratio; a t-test compares the means of two sets of continuous measurements.
parts.working: B1 categorical counts/observed vs expected; B1 t-test is for comparing means of continuous data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate χ² and state a conclusion.
parts.answer: χ² = 1.44; 1.44 < 3.84 (1 df), so the difference from 1 : 1 is not significant/due to chance; results fit the expected 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: B1 expected 200 each; B1 χ² = 1.44; B1 conclusion with 3.84.

practice.stem: A plant breeder thinks that seed coat colour in a variety of chickpea is controlled by one gene, with black seed coat dominant to cream. She crosses two plants that are both heterozygous.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the prediction she would make about the offspring if her hypothesis is correct.
parts.answer: 3 black : 1 cream (three-quarters black).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for a χ² test on her results.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the observed numbers of black and cream offspring and the numbers expected from a 3 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why she should grow a large number of offspring.
parts.answer: Ratios are probabilities; with large numbers, chance effects of random fertilisation are smaller and the test is more reliable.

practice.stem: Students will grow a non-pathogenic laboratory strain of E. coli on agar plates with and without lactose, and test for β-galactosidase activity using a colourless substrate that turns yellow when hydrolysed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two hazards in this investigation and describe a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Any two hazards with matched precautions: bacteria could be contaminated with pathogens/cause infection – use aseptic technique, flame loops, tape lids (do not seal fully), do not open plates after incubation, incubate at 25–30 °C not 37 °C; cultures spilt – disinfect bench before and after with disinfectant; disposal – autoclave cultures before disposal; Bunsen burner/hot loop – burns, tie hair back; chemical substrate/irritant – wear gloves and eye protection.
parts.working: B1 each hazard; B1 each matching precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plates are incubated at about 25 °C rather than 37 °C in school laboratories.
parts.answer: 37 °C (body temperature) favours growth of human pathogens that may have contaminated the plates.

practice.stem: Each human kidney contains about one million nephrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these parts of a nephron in the order in which filtrate passes through them: distal convoluted tubule, Bowman's capsule, collecting duct, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle.
parts.answer: Bowman's capsule → proximal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 if one pair is reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the region of the kidney (cortex or medulla) in which the glomeruli are found and the region in which most of each loop of Henle is found.
parts.answer: Glomeruli: cortex; loops of Henle: medulla.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that brings blood to a glomerulus and the vessel that carries blood away from it.
parts.answer: Afferent arteriole in; efferent arteriole out.
parts.working: B1 both needed.

practice.stem: Ali plays cricket for three hours in Lahore on a hot afternoon. He sweats a lot and eats salty pakoras, but drinks very little.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect on the water potential of Ali's blood.
parts.answer: It decreases (becomes more negative).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the changes in ADH secretion and in Ali's urine that follow.
parts.answer: More ADH is released from the posterior pituitary; the collecting ducts become more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood; a small volume of concentrated (dark) urine is produced.
parts.working: B1 more ADH. B1 more water reabsorbed in collecting duct / DCT. B1 small volume, more concentrated urine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ali then drinks a large glass of water. State how the volume of his urine will change over the next hour, and why.
parts.answer: The volume will increase (dilute urine); blood water potential rises, so less ADH is released and less water is reabsorbed in the collecting ducts.
parts.working: B1 more urine / dilute. B1 less ADH / collecting duct less permeable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how ultrafiltration takes place in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, so blood in the glomerulus is at high hydrostatic pressure; water and small solutes are forced out through gaps (fenestrations) in the capillary endothelium; the basement membrane acts as the filter, holding back large proteins (relative molecular mass above about 69 000) and cells; the fluid passes between the podocytes' foot processes (filtration slits) into the capsule space.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: afferent wider than efferent; high hydrostatic pressure; pores / fenestrations in endothelium; basement membrane is the filter; large proteins and blood cells retained; podocytes with filtration slits; filtrate contains water, glucose, urea, ions, amino acids.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the filtrate in Bowman's capsule has a lower concentration of protein than blood plasma but the same concentration of glucose.
parts.answer: Proteins are too large to pass through the basement membrane, so they stay in the blood; glucose molecules are small and pass freely, so their concentration is the same as in plasma.
parts.working: B1 proteins too large / retained by basement membrane. B1 glucose small, filtered freely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule.
parts.answer: Na⁺/K⁺ pumps in the basal membrane of the tubule cells actively pump Na⁺ out into the tissue fluid/blood, using ATP; this lowers the Na⁺ concentration inside the cell; Na⁺ diffuses into the cell from the lumen through cotransporter proteins that carry glucose with it (indirect active transport / cotransport); glucose then moves out of the cell into the blood by facilitated diffusion through the basal membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: Na⁺/K⁺ pump on basal membrane; uses ATP / active; low Na⁺ concentration in cell; Na⁺ moves in by facilitated diffusion with glucose (cotransporter / symporter); glucose against its concentration gradient; glucose leaves by facilitated diffusion into capillaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the structure of the proximal convoluted tubule cells is adapted for reabsorption.
parts.answer: Microvilli on the luminal surface give a large surface area for transport proteins; many mitochondria supply ATP for active transport.
parts.working: B1 microvilli → large surface area. B1 many mitochondria → ATP for active transport. (Also accept: many cotransporter proteins / tight junctions.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a fall in the water potential of the blood is detected and how ADH is released.
parts.answer: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall in water potential (they lose water and shrink); neurosecretory cells (in the hypothalamus) send impulses so ADH is released from the posterior pituitary gland into the blood.
parts.working: B1 osmoreceptors in hypothalamus. B1 ADH released from posterior pituitary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water.
parts.answer: ADH binds to receptors on the cell surface membrane of collecting duct cells; this activates adenylyl cyclase, producing cAMP as a second messenger; cAMP activates a protein kinase (cascade) that phosphorylates proteins; vesicles containing aquaporins move to and fuse with the luminal membrane; more aquaporins in the membrane allow more water to move out by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: ADH binds to receptor (on membrane of collecting duct cells); adenylyl cyclase activated / cAMP produced (second messenger); protein kinase activated / phosphorylation; vesicles with aquaporins; vesicles fuse with luminal (cell surface) membrane; more water channels → more water reabsorbed by osmosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this is an example of negative feedback.
parts.answer: The change (low water potential) triggers responses that reverse it – more water is reabsorbed so blood water potential rises back to the set point; as it returns to normal, less ADH is released.
parts.working: B1 response reverses the change / returns to set point. B1 less ADH once water potential is restored.

practice.stem: In a healthy adult the kidneys produce glomerular filtrate at a rate of 125 cm³ per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of filtrate produced per day in dm³.
parts.answer: 180 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The person produces 1.5 dm³ of urine per day. Calculate the percentage of the filtrate that is reabsorbed. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person with kidney failure who is treated by dialysis must limit how much water and salt they consume.
parts.answer: Their kidneys cannot remove excess water and salt (cannot form urine normally), so these build up in the blood between dialysis sessions, raising blood volume / pressure and causing oedema.
parts.working: B1 kidneys cannot excrete excess water / salt. B1 build-up → high blood pressure / oedema / fluid overload.

practice.stem:
In diabetes insipidus the posterior pituitary gland releases little or no ADH. A patient with this condition used a nasal spray of desmopressin, a drug that acts on the collecting duct in the same way as ADH. Her rate of urine production was measured.
Time after spray / h: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12
Urine production / cm³ min⁻¹: 10.0, 6.5, 2.0, 1.2, 1.5, 4.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before the spray, the patient produced urine at 10.0 cm³ min⁻¹. Calculate the volume of urine she would produce in one day at this rate, in dm³.
parts.answer: 14.4 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person who makes no ADH produces a large volume of dilute urine.
parts.answer: Without ADH, few aquaporins are inserted into the luminal membranes of the collecting duct cells (vesicles containing aquaporins stay in the cytoplasm); so the collecting duct walls have low permeability to water; little water moves out by osmosis into the medulla (even though its water potential is low), so a large volume of dilute urine passes out.
