Vessel P: wall thickness 1.2 mm, lumen diameter 4.0 mm, wall contains many elastic fibres.
Vessel Q: wall thickness 0.4 mm, lumen diameter 6.0 mm, flaps of tissue seen inside.
Vessel R: seen only with the microscope; wall one cell thick, lumen just wide enough for one red blood cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of wall thickness to lumen diameter for vessel P and for vessel Q. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify vessels P and Q and give a reason for each.
parts.answer: P is an artery – thick wall relative to lumen, with much elastic tissue; Q is a vein – thin wall, wide lumen, with valves.
parts.working: B1 P artery with reason. B1 Q vein with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why vessel R cannot be measured with a ruler and identify it.
parts.answer: R is a capillary; its diameter (about 8 µm) is too small to measure with a ruler – it needs a microscope with an eyepiece graticule.
parts.working: B1 capillary. B1 microscopic size / needs graticule / microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how arterioles can change the amount of blood flowing to a particular organ.
parts.answer: Arterioles have smooth muscle in their walls; contraction narrows the lumen (vasoconstriction), reducing flow to the organ; relaxation widens it (vasodilation), increasing flow.
parts.working: B1 smooth muscle in wall. B1 contraction narrows / relaxation widens lumen, changing flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During a cricket match, blood flow to leg muscles increases but blood flow to the gut decreases. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Leg muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose (and removal of CO₂/heat), so their arterioles dilate; digestion is less urgent, so gut arterioles constrict and blood is redirected.
parts.working: B1 muscles need more O₂ / glucose / remove CO₂. B1 blood redistributed / limited cardiac output shared.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why large arteries contain a lot of collagen in their outer layer.
parts.answer: Collagen is strong and resists the high pressure, so the artery does not burst / overstretch.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in blood pressure as blood flows from the aorta to the vena cava.
parts.answer: Pressure is highest and fluctuates (pulses) in the aorta and large arteries; it falls through the arterioles (largest fall) and the fluctuations disappear; it continues to fall through capillaries and venules, and is lowest (near zero) in the vena cava.
parts.working: B1 high and fluctuating in arteries. B1 large drop in arterioles, continues falling to lowest in veins / fluctuations lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The speed of blood flow is lowest in the capillaries, although each capillary is very narrow. Explain why, and why this is an advantage.
parts.answer: There are so many capillaries that their total cross-sectional area is much larger than that of the arteries; the same volume per second flows through a larger total area, so speed falls; slow flow gives more time for exchange of substances (oxygen, glucose, CO₂) with tissues.
parts.working: B1 very large total cross-sectional area. B1 same volume flow spread over larger area → lower velocity. B1 more time for exchange / diffusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the speed of blood increases again in the veins.
parts.answer: Capillaries join into fewer, larger vessels, so the total cross-sectional area decreases.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how tissue fluid is formed at the arterial end of a capillary.
parts.answer: Hydrostatic (blood) pressure is high at the arterial end; it is greater than the tendency of water to enter by osmosis (plasma has a lower water potential due to proteins); so water and small solutes (glucose, ions, oxygen) are forced out through gaps in the capillary wall; large plasma proteins and red cells stay in the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: high hydrostatic pressure; greater than the opposing water potential / osmotic effect; fluid forced out through gaps / pores in endothelium; small molecules leave (e.g. glucose, amino acids, ions); proteins / red blood cells remain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how much of this fluid returns to the blood at the venous end.
parts.answer: Hydrostatic pressure has fallen at the venous end; the plasma still has a lower water potential than tissue fluid because of the plasma proteins, so water moves back in by osmosis.
parts.working: B1 lower hydrostatic pressure. B1 water re-enters by osmosis down water potential gradient (due to plasma proteins).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the tissue fluid that does not return to the capillaries.
parts.answer: It drains into lymph capillaries / lymph vessels and is returned to the blood (in veins near the heart).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: Some children in areas affected by famine have diets very low in protein. Their blood plasma contains less protein than normal, and their legs and abdomen become swollen with fluid (oedema).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a low concentration of protein in blood plasma causes tissue fluid to build up.
parts.answer: With less protein, the water potential of the plasma is higher (less negative); the water potential gradient from tissue fluid to plasma at the venous end is smaller; so less water returns to the capillaries by osmosis, and more fluid stays in the tissues than the lymph can remove.
parts.working: B1 plasma water potential higher / less negative. B1 less water re-enters by osmosis at venous end. B1 more tissue fluid remains / lymph system cannot drain it all.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why people with very high blood pressure can also develop swelling of the ankles.
parts.answer: Higher hydrostatic pressure in capillaries forces more fluid out (and less returns at the venous end); in the legs gravity also raises pressure in the veins/capillaries, so fluid accumulates in the ankles.
parts.working: B1 more fluid forced out by higher hydrostatic pressure. B1 less reabsorbed / gravity effect in legs.

practice.stem: Students at a school in Peshawar want to find out how the intensity of exercise affects heart rate immediately after exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method to investigate the effect of exercise intensity on heart rate. Your method should allow reliable results to be collected.
parts.answer: Use step-ups on a bench of fixed height at different rates set by a metronome (e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 steps per minute) for a fixed time (e.g. 3 min); measure resting pulse first (count at the wrist for 30 s, ×2) and wait until it returns to resting between trials; measure pulse immediately after each bout; use the same person (or a group matched for age, sex, fitness); repeat each intensity three times on different days or after full recovery and calculate means; record results in a table and plot heart rate against step rate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: at least five intensities set precisely (metronome / treadmill speed); fixed duration of exercise; same step height; resting heart rate measured first; pulse counted for a stated time with a stated method (or pulse meter); measured immediately after exercise; allow return to resting rate between trials; same subject or matched subjects (age / sex / fitness / no caffeine); repeats and means; safety – stop if unwell / subjects in good health.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one ethical consideration when planning this investigation.
parts.answer: Volunteers must give informed consent and may withdraw at any time / people with heart or breathing problems should not take part.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the dependent variable and suggest one variable that cannot easily be controlled.
parts.answer: Dependent: heart rate (beats per minute); uncontrolled: e.g. emotional state / time since last meal / sleep.
parts.working: B1 both.

practice.stem: Daphnia (water fleas) are transparent, so their heart can be seen beating under a microscope. A student wants to test the hypothesis that higher concentrations of caffeine increase the heart rate of Daphnia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method the student could use to investigate the effect of caffeine concentration on the heart rate of Daphnia.
parts.answer: Prepare caffeine solutions by dilution of a stock, e.g. 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mg cm⁻³, using pond water; place one Daphnia on a cavity slide with a small drop of pond water, remove excess water, view under low power; let it acclimatise for 2–3 minutes and count the resting heart rate (e.g. beats in 20 s, ×3); replace the water with a fixed volume of caffeine solution, wait a fixed time (e.g. 5 min) and count again; keep temperature constant (e.g. temperature of room checked / avoid heat from lamp – use LED or limit time under light); use different Daphnia of similar size for each concentration, at least 5 per concentration, and calculate the mean change.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: at least five concentrations including 0 (control) made by dilution; same volume of solution; acclimatisation / fixed exposure time; heart rate counted for a fixed period with method (tally / counter / video slowed down); resting rate measured for each animal before treatment (or calculate % change); temperature controlled (lamp heat avoided, water bath for solutions); similar size / age of Daphnia; fresh Daphnia for each trial; replicates and mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Daphnia are small invertebrates. Suggest two ways the student can act ethically in this investigation.
parts.answer: Use the minimum number of animals; keep exposure short and return them to pond water afterwards; avoid overheating under the microscope lamp; handle gently with a wide pipette.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A student counts the heartbeats of Daphnia placed in pond water at 10 °C, 15 °C, 20 °C, 25 °C and 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: temperature of the water. Dependent: heart rate of Daphnia (beats per minute).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could control the temperature of the water around the Daphnia.
parts.answer: Keep the pond water samples in thermostatic water baths at each temperature; check the temperature of the drop on the slide with a thermometer/temperature probe; use a cold light source so the lamp does not heat the slide; count quickly.
parts.working: B1 water baths at set temperatures. B1 avoid lamp heating / measure temperature on slide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other variables that should be standardised.
parts.answer: Size/age of Daphnia; time allowed to acclimatise before counting; duration of count; volume of water on the slide; source of Daphnia.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: Students measured pulse rate after a 2-minute run by finding the pulse at the wrist, counting beats for 15 s and multiplying by 4. Sometimes counting started up to 20 s after the run ended.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three sources of error in this method.
parts.answer: Counting for only 15 s then ×4 multiplies any counting error by 4; a beat may be missed or counted twice at the start/end of the count; heart rate falls quickly after exercise, so a delay before counting lowers the reading; pulse may be hard to find; reaction time starting/stopping the timer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest improvements to reduce the errors you described.
parts.answer: Use a digital heart-rate monitor / pulse oximeter that reads continuously; count for 30 s or 60 s; start counting immediately (or record continuously and read the value at a fixed time after exercise); a partner times while the subject counts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two improvements matched to errors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why repeating the readings and calculating a mean improves the reliability but not the accuracy of a reading that is always taken 20 s late.
parts.answer: Repeats reduce the effect of random errors (variation between readings); a delay of 20 s every time is a systematic error, so every reading is lower by a similar amount and the mean is still too low.
parts.working: B1 repeats reduce random error. B1 systematic error not removed by averaging.

practice.stem:
Mean heart rate (beats per minute) of 8 trained athletes and 8 untrained students from the same college, before and after a 3-minute run:
Time: rest, 0 min after, 1 min, 2 min, 3 min, 4 min
Trained: 60, 150, 112, 84, 68, 61
Untrained: 78, 172, 150, 128, 110, 96

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the recovery of heart rate in the two groups.
parts.answer: Trained students had a lower resting rate (60 v 78) and a lower peak (150 v 172); trained students' heart rate fell faster – back to resting within 4 min, untrained still 18 beats above resting (96) after 4 min; both groups decreased most in the first minute.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three comparative points with data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that training causes faster recovery. Discuss whether this conclusion is valid.
parts.answer: The data are consistent with the conclusion (trained group recovers faster); but this is a comparison of two existing groups, so other differences (genetics, diet, body mass, sex) may explain it; only means are given with no spread/statistical test, and group sizes are small; a valid test would measure the same students before and after a training programme.
parts.working: B1 data support. B1 other variables / correlation not causation. B1 need spread / statistical test / sample size / before-and-after design.

practice.stem: A student counted 47 heartbeats of a Daphnia in 20 s. After caffeine solution was added she counted 58 beats in 20 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute before and after adding caffeine.
parts.answer: Before: 141 beats min⁻¹; after: 174 beats min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The caffeine solution was made by dissolving 0.40 g of caffeine in 250 cm³ of pond water. Calculate its concentration in mg cm⁻³.
parts.answer: 1.6 mg cm⁻³
parts.working: 400 mg ÷ 250 cm³ = 1.6 mg cm⁻³

practice.stem:
Percentage saturation of human haemoglobin at different partial pressures of oxygen (pO₂):
pO₂ / kPa: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12
Saturation / %: 10, 25, 45, 60, 72, 80, 90, 95, 97

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of graph you would draw and describe the shape of the curve you would expect.
parts.answer: Line graph with pO₂ on the x-axis and percentage saturation on the y-axis, points joined by a smooth curve; S-shaped (sigmoid) curve.
parts.working: B1 line graph, pO₂ on x-axis. B1 sigmoid / S-shaped smooth curve.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate, by linear interpolation between the readings, the partial pressure of oxygen at which haemoglobin is 50 % saturated. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 3.3 kPa
parts.working: M1 50 % lies between 3 kPa (45 %) and 4 kPa (60 %). A1 3 + (5 ÷ 15) × 1 = 3.3 kPa.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the curve is steepest between 2 kPa and 4 kPa.
parts.answer: Once one oxygen molecule has bound, the haemoglobin changes shape, making it easier for further oxygen molecules to bind (cooperative binding); so a small rise in pO₂ gives a large rise in saturation.
parts.working: B1 binding of first O₂ changes shape of haemoglobin. B1 increases affinity for further O₂ / cooperative binding.

practice.stem: A student plans to compare the resting heart rates of 15 hockey players and 15 students who do no regular exercise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Athletes have a lower mean resting heart rate than non-athletes (because training increases stroke volume).
parts.working: B1 directional, testable statement about the difference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis that would be tested with a t-test.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean resting heart rate of athletes and non-athletes.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a t-test is suitable for these data and Spearman's rank correlation is not.
parts.answer: The investigation compares the means of two groups / two independent samples of continuous data (approximately normally distributed); Spearman's rank tests for a correlation between two variables measured on the same individuals, which is not what is being asked.
parts.working: B1 t-test compares means of two groups (normal, continuous data). B1 Spearman's is for correlation / relationship between two variables.

practice.stem:
Mean red blood cell counts of healthy adults:
Karachi (sea level): 5.0 million per mm³
Villages in Hunza living at about 2,500 m for many years: 5.7 million per mm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference in red blood cell count between the two groups.
parts.answer: The partial pressure of oxygen in the air is lower at high altitude; so haemoglobin is less saturated and less oxygen reaches tissues; over time the body responds by producing more red blood cells in the bone marrow, increasing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
parts.working: B1 lower pO₂ at altitude. B1 less oxygen loaded / tissues receive less. B1 more red blood cells made (more haemoglobin), so more oxygen carried.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a disadvantage of having a very high red blood cell count.
parts.answer: The blood becomes more viscous, so the heart has to work harder / greater risk of blood clots.
parts.working: B1

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
Resting heart rates (beats per minute) of 10 students who train for football and 10 who do not:
Trained: 62, 58, 66, 60, 64, 59, 63, 61, 67, 60
Untrained: 68, 72, 65, 70, 74, 66, 71, 69, 75, 67
s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1));  t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation for each group. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Trained: s = 2.98; untrained: s = 3.33

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 with 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10. State what you can conclude.
parts.answer: 5.44 is greater than 2.10, so the null hypothesis is rejected: there is a significant difference between the mean resting heart rates (probability of the difference being due to chance is less than 5 %).
parts.working: B1 t > critical value so reject null hypothesis. B1 difference is significant / not due to chance at p < 0.05.

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

practice.stem: Since 2016, many cases of typhoid in Sindh have been caused by strains of Salmonella Typhi that are resistant to several antibiotics (extensively drug-resistant typhoid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic.
parts.answer: A random mutation produces an allele giving resistance (e.g. coding for an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic); when the antibiotic is used it acts as a selection pressure; bacteria without the allele are killed, resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (binary fission), passing on the allele; the allele frequency increases over generations; (resistance alleles on plasmids can also pass between bacteria by horizontal gene transfer/conjugation).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mutation (random, already present); antibiotic is the selection pressure; resistant survive and reproduce; allele passed to offspring; allele frequency increases; plasmid transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria can be reduced.
parts.answer: Any two of: use antibiotics only when needed/prescribed; complete the full course; avoid using antibiotics in animal feed; improve sanitation and clean drinking water; vaccination against typhoid; infection control/hand washing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by stabilising, directional and disruptive selection.
parts.answer: Stabilising: individuals with intermediate phenotypes are favoured, extremes selected against; the mean stays the same and variation decreases. Directional: individuals at one extreme are favoured; the mean shifts in that direction. Disruptive: both extremes are favoured over the intermediate; can produce two distinct groups.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Human birth mass is an example of stabilising selection. Explain why.
parts.answer: Babies of very low birth mass have a higher death rate (less able to keep warm/more infections) and very high birth mass increases complications in birth; intermediate birth masses have the highest survival, so the mean is maintained and variation is reduced.
parts.working: B1 extremes have higher mortality; B1 intermediate favoured/mean maintained.

practice.stem: Sahiwal cattle are a dairy breed from Punjab, valued for tolerating heat and resisting ticks. Breeders want to increase their milk yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how breeders could use artificial selection to increase the milk yield of Sahiwal cattle over many generations.
parts.answer: Measure milk yield of cows and select those with the highest yield; bulls cannot be measured directly, so select bulls whose mothers/daughters (progeny testing) have high yields; breed selected cows with selected bulls (e.g. by artificial insemination); select the highest-yielding offspring and breed them; repeat over many generations so the frequency of alleles for high yield increases.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why breeders should also keep selecting for heat tolerance while selecting for milk yield.
parts.answer: Selecting only for yield may reduce/lose alleles for heat tolerance or tick resistance, which are needed in Pakistan's climate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one difference between artificial selection and natural selection.
parts.answer: In artificial selection humans choose which individuals breed, for characteristics useful to humans; in natural selection the environment/selection pressures decide which survive and reproduce.

practice.stem: Maize farmers in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa buy new hybrid maize seed every year. The seed is produced by crossing two inbred (homozygous) lines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the inbred lines are often small and produce low yields.
parts.answer: Repeated inbreeding increases homozygosity; harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be expressed in the homozygous state (inbreeding depression).
parts.working: B1 homozygous; B1 harmful recessive alleles expressed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the F1 hybrid plants are vigorous and uniform.
parts.answer: Hybrids are heterozygous at many loci, so harmful recessive alleles are masked (hybrid vigour); both parents are homozygous, so all F1 plants have the same genotype and are uniform.
parts.working: B1 heterozygous/hybrid vigour; B1 identical genotypes, uniform.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why farmers do not save seed from their hybrid crop to sow the next year.
parts.answer: Seed from F1 × F1 is the F2 generation; alleles segregate, producing many different genotypes, so plants are not uniform and many have lower yield.
parts.working: B1 segregation/variety of genotypes in F2; B1 not uniform/lower yield.

practice.stem: Stem rust is a fungal disease that can destroy wheat crops. Wheat breeders in Pakistan cross local high-yielding varieties with varieties that carry a resistance allele.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how breeders could produce a high-yielding variety that is resistant to stem rust.
parts.answer: Cross a high-yielding variety with a resistant variety; grow offspring and expose them to the fungus, selecting plants that are resistant and have high yield; breed these together/backcross to the high-yielding parent for several generations, selecting each time, until the variety is true-breeding for both features.
parts.working: B1 cross the two varieties; B1 select resistant, high-yield offspring (test by infecting); B1 repeat for many generations/backcrossing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: New races of the stem rust fungus sometimes appear that can infect previously resistant wheat. Explain how this happens.
parts.answer: Mutation in the fungus produces a new allele allowing it to infect resistant wheat; widely planted resistant wheat is a selection pressure; fungi with the new allele reproduce, so the new race spreads/allele frequency increases.
parts.working: B1 mutation in fungus; B1 resistant wheat selects for it; B1 the new race survives, reproduces and spreads.

practice.stem: Rock pocket mice live in deserts in North America. Most mice living on pale sandy rock have pale fur; most mice living on dark lava flows have dark fur. Dark fur is caused by a dominant allele of the Mc1r gene. Owls, which hunt by sight, are their main predators.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how natural selection has led to most mice on lava flows having dark fur.
parts.answer: There is variation in fur colour in the population, caused by different alleles; owls see and catch pale mice more easily on dark rock (predation is the selection pressure); dark mice are camouflaged, so more survive and reproduce; they pass on the dark allele, so its frequency increases over generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: variation/alleles; predation as selection pressure; dark mice survive and reproduce; allele passed on/frequency increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a new dominant mutation for dark fur could spread through a population faster than a new recessive mutation would.
parts.answer: A dominant allele is expressed in heterozygotes, so it shows in the phenotype immediately and is selected for at once; a recessive allele is hidden in heterozygotes and only selected when homozygous, which is rare at first.
parts.working: B1 dominant expressed in heterozygote/visible to selection; B1 recessive hidden until homozygous.

practice.stem: Mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles transmit malaria. In one district, the same insecticide was sprayed in houses every year. The percentage of mosquitoes surviving a standard dose was: year 1 – 2 %; year 3 – 9 %; year 5 – 31 %; year 7 – 68 %. Spraying then stopped. In year 10 the survival was 40 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the change in survival between years 1 and 7.
parts.answer: Some mosquitoes already carried a resistance allele (from mutation) at a low frequency (2 % survival); the insecticide killed non-resistant mosquitoes – a selection pressure; resistant mosquitoes survived and reproduced, passing on the allele; the frequency of the resistance allele increased each generation (directional selection), so survival rose to 68 %.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: pre-existing allele/mutation; selection pressure; survivors reproduce; allele passed on; allele frequency increases; directional selection; use of data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why survival fell between year 7 and year 10.
parts.answer: Without insecticide there is no advantage to resistance; the resistance allele may carry a cost (e.g. lower fertility or slower development), so non-resistant mosquitoes are selected for/out-reproduce resistant ones and the allele frequency falls.
parts.working: B1 no selection for resistance; B1 resistant individuals at a disadvantage without insecticide.

practice.stem: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by the allele Hbˢ. People with genotype HbˢHbˢ have sickle cell anaemia; heterozygotes (HbᴬHbˢ) are mostly healthy and are less likely to die from severe malaria than HbᴬHbᴬ people. The Hbˢ allele is much more common in parts of Africa where malaria is common than in places without malaria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Hbˢ allele remains at a high frequency in areas where malaria is common.
parts.answer: HbˢHbˢ people often die young/have fewer children, so Hbˢ alleles are lost; HbᴬHbᴬ people are more likely to die of malaria, so Hbᴬ alleles are lost; heterozygotes have a selective advantage – they survive malaria and reproduce, passing on both alleles; so both alleles are kept in the population (balanced polymorphism/heterozygote advantage).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: selection against HbˢHbˢ; selection against HbᴬHbᴬ by malaria; heterozygote advantage; both alleles maintained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the frequency of Hbˢ is falling slowly among descendants of people who moved from these areas to countries without malaria.
parts.answer: Malaria is no longer a selection pressure, so heterozygotes have no advantage; HbˢHbˢ individuals are still selected against, so the allele frequency falls slowly (slowly because most Hbˢ alleles are carried in heterozygotes, where they are not selected against).
parts.working: B1 no heterozygote advantage without malaria; B1 selection against homozygotes only, so slow decline.

practice.stem: On an island, a severe drought killed most plants that produce small, soft seeds, leaving mainly large, hard seeds. The mean beak depth of a population of seed-eating finches was 9.2 mm before the drought and 9.7 mm in the generation hatched after it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of selection shown and explain how the change happened.
parts.answer: Directional selection; beak depth varies and is partly genetic (polygenic); during the drought only birds with deeper beaks could crack the large, hard seeds; so they survived and bred, while birds with shallow beaks starved; alleles for deep beaks were passed on, so the mean in the next generation increased.
parts.working: B1 directional; B1 variation with genetic basis; B1 deep-beaked birds survived/reproduced (food as selection pressure); B1 alleles passed on/mean shifted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change in mean beak depth would not have occurred if beak depth were controlled only by the environment.
parts.answer: Characteristics caused only by the environment are not inherited, so offspring would not show the change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'species' using the biological species concept.
parts.answer: A group of organisms with similar features that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring, and are reproductively isolated from other such groups.
parts.working: B1 interbreed to produce fertile offspring; B1 reproductively isolated from other species.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between allopatric speciation and sympatric speciation.
parts.answer: Allopatric: populations are separated by a geographical barrier. Sympatric: a new species forms in the same area without geographical separation (e.g. by polyploidy or behavioural isolation).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between genetic drift and natural selection.
parts.answer: Drift is random/due to chance, selection is non-random (depends on phenotype and environment); drift has most effect in small populations, selection acts in any size population; selection leads to adaptation, drift does not.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both processes change the gene pool of a population.
parts.answer: Both change the frequency of alleles in the population from one generation to the next; alleles can be lost or become fixed.
parts.working: B1 change allele frequencies; B1 alleles lost/fixed.

practice.stem: A species of freshwater fish lived in one large lake. Over thousands of years the water level fell and the lake split into two smaller lakes, one with clear, rocky water and one with muddy water and dense weed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how two separate species of fish could evolve from the original population.
parts.answer: The two populations are geographically isolated, so no gene flow/interbreeding between them; different mutations arise in each population; different selection pressures in each lake (e.g. food, predators, water clarity) favour different alleles; genetic drift may also change allele frequencies (especially in small populations); over many generations the gene pools become so different that the two populations could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring even if they met (reproductive isolation) – allopatric speciation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: geographical isolation; no gene flow; different mutations; different selection pressures (with example); drift; allele frequencies change; reproductive isolation/cannot produce fertile offspring.

practice.stem: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is hexaploid with 2n = 42. It is thought to have arisen when tetraploid emmer wheat (2n = 28) hybridised with a wild grass, Aegilops tauschii (2n = 14).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of chromosomes in the hybrid formed from one gamete of each parent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this hybrid was sterile.
parts.answer: The chromosomes from the two parents are not homologous, so they cannot pair up in prophase I of meiosis; viable gametes cannot be formed.
parts.working: B1 chromosomes not homologous/cannot pair; B1 meiosis fails/no functional gametes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a fertile hexaploid species could have formed from the hybrid in the same place as its parents, and why this is an example of sympatric speciation.
parts.answer: The chromosome number of the hybrid doubled (e.g. a failure of cell division/non-disjunction), giving 42; every chromosome now has a homologous partner, so meiosis works and fertile gametes form; the new plant cannot produce fertile offspring with either parent, so it is reproductively isolated without any geographical barrier.
parts.working: B1 chromosome doubling to 42; B1 homologues can pair/fertile; B1 reproductively isolated in same area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by genetic drift.
parts.answer: A random (chance) change in allele frequencies in a population from one generation to the next, not caused by selection; it has a larger effect in small populations.
parts.working: B1 random/chance change in allele frequency; B1 greater effect in small populations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A storm carried six birds of one species to a remote island where none of that species lived. Over 200 years the island population grew to several thousand. Explain why the island population may show less genetic diversity and different allele frequencies from the mainland population (the founder effect).
parts.answer: The six founders carried only a small sample of the alleles in the mainland gene pool; by chance some alleles were absent and others at a higher frequency than on the mainland; the population grew from these few, so it has lower diversity; drift in the small early population changed frequencies further.
parts.working: B1 founders carry a small/non-representative sample of alleles; B1 some alleles lost/frequencies different by chance; B1 low diversity as population grows from few individuals/drift.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a population with low genetic diversity may be at greater risk of extinction.
parts.answer: Fewer alleles means less variation for natural selection to act on if the environment changes (e.g. a new disease).

practice.stem: The amino acid sequence of a respiratory protein, 104 amino acids long, was compared between humans and four other species. Number of amino acid differences from the human sequence: species K – 0; species L – 1; species M – 12; species N – 21.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of amino acids in species M's protein that are identical to the human sequence. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these data provide evidence about the evolutionary relationships of the species.
parts.answer: Differences in amino acid sequence result from mutations in DNA that build up over time; the fewer differences, the more recently the species shared a common ancestor; so K and L are most closely related to humans, and N is the most distantly related.
parts.working: B1 mutations accumulate over time; B1 fewer differences = more recent common ancestor; B1 correct order using data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why comparing DNA base sequences of the gene gives more information than comparing amino acid sequences.
parts.answer: The genetic code is degenerate, so some base changes do not change the amino acid; these silent mutations (and changes in introns/non-coding DNA) are detected only by DNA comparison.
parts.working: B1 degenerate code/silent mutations; B1 non-coding DNA also compared.

practice.stem:
Scientists compared a 30-base section of mitochondrial DNA from three populations of a mountain goat (markhor) from different valleys.
Population X: ATGCTAGCCTTAGGACATCCGTTAGCAATC
Population Y: ATGCTGGCCTTAGGATATCCGCTAGCAATT
Population Z: ATACTGGCTTTAGGATATCCACTGGCGATT

parts.label: a
parts.text: Count the number of base differences between X and Y, X and Z, and Y and Z.
parts.working: B2 all three correct (B1 for two).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to state which two populations are most closely related and explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: X and Y; they have the fewest base differences, so fewest mutations have built up since they shared a common ancestor/they separated most recently.
parts.working: B1 X and Y; B1 reasoning.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why mitochondrial DNA is useful for studying relationships between populations of the same species.
parts.answer: It is inherited only from the mother, so it does not undergo recombination/crossing over; it mutates relatively quickly, so differences build up even between closely related populations.
parts.working: B1 maternal inheritance/no recombination; B1 fast mutation rate.

practice.stem: A horse (2n = 64) and a donkey (2n = 62) can mate to produce a mule. Mules are strong and healthy but almost always sterile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of chromosomes in a body cell of a mule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why mules are sterile.
parts.answer: The mule has an odd number of chromosomes and the horse and donkey chromosomes are not all homologous; they cannot pair correctly in prophase I of meiosis; so gametes have unbalanced/incorrect chromosome sets and are not viable.
parts.working: B1 odd number/non-homologous chromosomes; B1 cannot pair in meiosis I; B1 viable gametes not formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Horses and donkeys are separate species even though they can produce offspring. Explain why, and name this type of reproductive isolating mechanism.
parts.answer: Their offspring are sterile, so genes cannot pass between the two gene pools; postzygotic isolation (hybrid sterility).
parts.working: B1 offspring not fertile/no gene flow; B1 postzygotic/hybrid sterility.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between continuous variation and discontinuous variation, giving one example of each in humans.
parts.answer: Continuous: a range of values with no distinct categories (e.g. height, mass); discontinuous: distinct categories with no intermediates (e.g. ABO blood group).
parts.working: B1 continuous description; B1 discontinuous description; B1 correct examples of both.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why continuous variation is usually affected by both genes and the environment.
parts.answer: It is controlled by many genes (polygenes) each having a small additive effect; the environment (e.g. diet) also affects how the genes are expressed, adding to the range of phenotypes.
parts.working: B1 polygenic/many genes with additive effect; B1 environment modifies phenotype.

practice.stem:
The lengths (cm) of eight leaflets taken from one neem tree were: 6.2, 5.8, 7.1, 6.5, 6.9, 5.5, 6.0, 6.8.
Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the leaflet lengths. Give the standard deviation to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: mean 6.35 cm; s = 0.57 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second tree had leaflets with mean length 6.40 cm and standard deviation 1.20 cm. Explain what the two standard deviations show.
parts.answer: The means are similar but the second tree has a much larger spread of leaflet lengths/more variation around the mean; the first tree's leaflets are more uniform.
parts.working: B1 means similar; B1 larger SD = more spread/variation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why leaflets on one tree vary in length even though they all have the same genotype.
parts.answer: Environmental factors differ for each leaflet, e.g. light (shade), position, age.

practice.stem: A researcher compared the mass at birth of lambs from two breeds of sheep. She calculated t = 1.45 with 18 degrees of freedom. The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 18 df is 2.10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null hypothesis that was tested.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean birth mass of lambs of the two breeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the researcher can conclude, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 1.45 < 2.10, so the probability that the difference is due to chance is greater than 0.05; accept the null hypothesis – there is no significant difference in mean birth mass.
parts.working: B1 t below critical value; B1 accept null/no significant difference.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two conditions that the data should meet for a t-test to be suitable.
parts.answer: Any two of: data are continuous measurements; data are approximately normally distributed; two independent samples being compared; samples should have similar variances; sample size less than about 30 per group.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem:
Shell lengths (mm) of a species of land snail were measured on an exposed hillside and in a sheltered valley.
Hillside: 18.2, 19.5, 17.8, 20.1, 18.9, 19.4, 18.6, 19.9 (mean 19.05, s = 0.816)
Valley: 16.9, 17.5, 16.2, 18.0, 17.1, 16.6, 17.8, 16.4 (mean 17.06, s = 0.659)
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2.
Critical values of t at p = 0.05: 12 df – 2.18; 14 df – 2.14; 16 df – 2.12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of t. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of degrees of freedom and what the student can conclude.
parts.answer: 14 df; 5.36 > 2.14, so the difference between the mean shell lengths is significant (p < 0.05) – hillside snails have longer shells; reject the null hypothesis.
parts.working: B1 14 df and comparison with 2.14; B1 significant difference/reject null.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the result does not show that the difference is genetic.
parts.answer: The difference could be caused by environmental factors (e.g. food or calcium availability, temperature) rather than different alleles.

practice.stem: Albinism is caused by a recessive allele. In one population, 1 in every 2500 people has albinism. The Hardy–Weinberg equations are p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the recessive allele, q, and of the dominant allele, p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the population who are heterozygous carriers. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two conditions that must apply for the Hardy–Weinberg principle to give reliable estimates.
parts.answer: Any two of: large population; random mating; no mutation; no migration in or out; no selection for or against any allele.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A gene in a population of 800 wild rats has two alleles, A and a. A survey found 410 AA, 300 Aa and 90 aa individuals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequencies of alleles A and a in this population.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Hardy–Weinberg equation to calculate the expected numbers of AA, Aa and aa rats.
parts.working: M1 p² × 800, 2pq × 800, q² × 800; A1 all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compare the observed and expected numbers, and suggest one explanation for the difference.
parts.answer: Fewer heterozygotes and more homozygotes than expected; this could be due to non-random mating/inbreeding (e.g. a small, isolated colony), or selection against heterozygotes.
parts.working: B1 comparison; B1 valid explanation.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
The tail length of field mice was measured on two islands.
Island A: mean 42.6 mm, standard deviation 3.2 mm, n = 25
Island B: mean 45.1 mm, standard deviation 3.6 mm, n = 36
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n. The 95 % confidence interval is approximately mean ± 2 × SE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the standard error and the 95 % confidence interval for each island.
parts.working: B1 both SE; M1 mean ± 2SE; A1 both intervals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the confidence intervals suggest about the difference between the two populations.
parts.answer: The intervals do not overlap, so the difference between the mean tail lengths is likely to be significant (real, not due to chance); island B mice have longer tails. (A statistical test would confirm this.)
parts.working: B1 no overlap; B1 likely significant difference.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student measured the wing length (mm) of house sparrows caught and released in a rural area and in the centre of Karachi.
Rural: 76.2, 77.5, 75.8, 78.1, 76.9, 77.3
City: 74.9, 75.6, 74.1, 76.0, 75.2, 74.6
t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation (n − 1) of each sample. Give means to 2 decimal places and standard deviations to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: B1 means; M1 method for s; A1 both s values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate t to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 substitution; A1 4.25.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 10 df is 2.23. Explain what the result shows.
parts.answer: 4.25 > 2.23, so the difference between the means is significant; there is less than a 5 % probability that it is due to chance; rural sparrows have longer wings.
parts.working: B1 comparison with 2.23; B1 significant, rural longer.

practice.stem:
A hospital laboratory recorded the percentage of Salmonella Typhi samples resistant to the antibiotic ciprofloxacin, and the number of ciprofloxacin prescriptions in the city (thousands per year).
Year 1: 12 %, 140; Year 2: 18 %, 165; Year 3: 27 %, 190; Year 4: 41 %, 230; Year 5: 55 %, 260.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the proportion of resistant samples between year 1 and year 5. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student concludes that 'increasing use of ciprofloxacin caused the increase in resistance'. Evaluate this conclusion.
parts.answer: Support: both increase together (positive correlation) and greater use means stronger selection pressure for resistant bacteria. Against: correlation does not prove cause; no statistical test done; only five years of data from one city; other factors (e.g. resistant strains arriving with travellers, spread through contaminated water, which samples were sent for testing) could be involved.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation/consistent with selection; B1 correlation not causation; B1 one other valid limitation.

practice.stem:
A species of land snail has yellow-shelled and brown-shelled forms. Thrushes eat the snails, smashing the shells on stones. Students counted live snails and broken shells near thrush stones in two habitats.
Grassland – live: 160 yellow, 40 brown; broken shells: 22 yellow, 28 brown.
Woodland (dark leaf litter) – live: 45 yellow, 155 brown; broken shells: 31 yellow, 19 brown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each habitat, calculate the percentage of live snails that are yellow and the percentage of broken shells that are yellow.
parts.answer: Grassland: live 80 % yellow, broken 44 % yellow; woodland: live 22.5 % yellow, broken 62 % yellow
parts.working: B2 all four (B1 for two).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use these results to explain the distribution of the two forms.
parts.answer: In each habitat, the less common form is over-represented among broken shells (eaten more than expected): brown in grassland, yellow in woodland; thrushes hunt by sight, so the form that contrasts with the background is seen and eaten more; the camouflaged form survives and reproduces, so its frequency is higher in that habitat (natural selection by predation).
parts.working: B1 use of data showing selective predation; B1 conspicuous form eaten more; B1 camouflaged form survives/reproduces – higher frequency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the results from the broken shells might not fully represent the snails eaten by thrushes.
parts.answer: Some snails are eaten elsewhere/not at stones; other predators take snails; old shells may remain from earlier seasons; brown shells may be harder to find.

practice.stem: To investigate selection by birds, students made 100 green and 100 brown 'caterpillars' from modelling clay and placed them on the grass of a school field in one afternoon. The next morning they counted those with beak marks: green 14, brown 31. They concluded that birds select against brown caterpillars on grass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three limitations of this investigation that reduce confidence in the conclusion.
parts.answer: Any three of: only one trial/one day; done on one field only; marks may be made by other animals (e.g. rodents, insects) not birds; clay models do not behave or smell like real caterpillars; models may have been moved or lost; identification of beak marks is subjective; models may not have been placed randomly; no statistical test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three improvements.
parts.answer: Any three matching improvements: repeat on several days/sites; place models at random positions (random coordinates); use a standard key/photographs to identify bird beak marks, or have the same person check all; place an equal number on another background (e.g. bare soil) as a comparison; count marks after a fixed time; use a χ² test to see if the difference is significant.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A student wants to find out whether bacteria from a culture become more resistant to an antibacterial chemical after repeated exposure. She has a non-pathogenic bacterium, nutrient agar plates, sterile paper discs, the antibacterial chemical at 10 % concentration, sterile distilled water and normal microbiology apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method she could use. Your method should be safe and allow valid conclusions to be drawn.
parts.answer: Points: aseptic technique (flame loop/neck of bottle, work near Bunsen, lid lifted only slightly); spread a standard volume of culture evenly on agar (lawn); place discs soaked in a series of concentrations (dilute 10 % stock, e.g. 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10 %) and a control disc with sterile water; incubate at 25 °C for a set time (e.g. 48 h), lids taped not sealed; measure diameter of clear zone of inhibition with a ruler (two diameters at right angles, mean); take bacteria from the edge of the clear zone around a disc, grow them, and repeat the exposure for several 'generations'; compare inhibition zone size at each round (smaller zone = more resistance); keep agar depth/volume, temperature, disc size and soaking time constant; at least three plates per round, calculate means; dispose of plates by autoclaving.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven points; credit specific detail.

practice.stem: Students compare how two non-pathogenic laboratory strains of a bacterium (strain P and strain Q) respond to the same antibiotic, using paper discs on agar plates and measuring the diameter of the clear zone around each disc.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent and dependent variables.
parts.answer: Independent: strain of bacterium (P or Q); dependent: diameter of the clear zone (zone of inhibition).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three variables that must be standardised.
parts.answer: Any three of: concentration of antibiotic; size of paper disc/volume of antibiotic on disc; volume and density of bacteria spread; depth/type of agar; incubation temperature; incubation time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: A disc soaked in sterile distilled water (no antibiotic) placed on each plate; shows that any clear zone is caused by the antibiotic and not by the disc or handling.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 purpose.
