subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the terms 'source' and 'sink' in translocation.
parts.answer: Source: a part of the plant where assimilates (sucrose) are loaded into the phloem, e.g. a photosynthesising leaf or a storage organ being used. Sink: a part where assimilates are removed from the phloem and used or stored, e.g. a growing root tip, fruit or developing tuber.
parts.working: B1 source – where sucrose enters phloem/is produced or released; B1 sink – where sucrose leaves phloem/is used or stored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a sugarcane plant, state one example of a source and one example of a sink.
parts.answer: Source: mature photosynthesising leaf. Sink: the stem (storage of sucrose), growing shoot tip or roots.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the main carbohydrate transported in the phloem and suggest why it is transported in this form rather than as glucose.
parts.answer: Sucrose; it is non-reducing/less reactive, so it is not used up (respired) on the way, and it is soluble so it can be carried in solution.
parts.working: B1 sucrose; B1 less reactive/not metabolised in transit (accept: soluble).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how sucrose is loaded into a sieve tube element from a companion cell in a leaf.
parts.answer: Companion cells use ATP to actively pump H⁺ ions out (proton pump); this sets up a H⁺ concentration gradient; H⁺ diffuses back into the companion cell through a cotransporter protein carrying sucrose with it (cotransport); sucrose then passes into the sieve tube element through plasmodesmata (down its concentration gradient).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: H⁺ pumped out using ATP; H⁺ gradient; cotransporter protein with sucrose; via plasmodesmata into sieve tube.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how loading sucrose at the source causes mass flow of phloem sap towards a sink.
parts.answer: Sucrose loading lowers the water potential in the sieve tube; water enters by osmosis from the xylem/surrounding cells, raising hydrostatic pressure at the source; at the sink sucrose is removed, water leaves, so pressure is lower; sap flows down the hydrostatic pressure gradient from high to low pressure.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: water potential lowered; water enters by osmosis; high hydrostatic pressure at source; lower pressure at sink; flow down pressure gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process in translocation uses ATP directly?
A movement of sucrose through sieve plates
B pumping of hydrogen ions out of companion cells
C movement of water from xylem into sieve tubes
D diffusion of sucrose through plasmodesmata
parts.answer: B pumping of hydrogen ions out of companion cells
parts.working: Proton pumps in companion cell membranes hydrolyse ATP to move H⁺ out; the H⁺ gradient then drives sucrose cotransport. Movement of water into the sieve tubes (C) is osmosis, a passive process.

practice.stem: A gardener in Mirpurkhas removed a complete ring of bark (including the phloem but not the xylem) from a branch of a mango tree. After four weeks the bark just above the ring had swollen and the fruits below the ring on that branch were small.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the swelling above the ring.
parts.answer: The phloem has been removed, so sucrose/assimilates moving down from the leaves cannot pass the ring; they accumulate above it, and water enters by osmosis/the tissue grows, causing swelling.
parts.working: B1 phloem removed, translocation blocked; B1 sugars accumulate above ring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves on the branch did not wilt.
parts.answer: The xylem was not removed, so water and mineral ions still reach the leaves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fruits below the ring were small.
parts.answer: Fruits are sinks; the sucrose they need for growth/storage comes from leaves above the ring through the phloem, which is now cut, so less sucrose reaches them.
parts.working: B1 fruits are sinks; B1 supply of sucrose from source cut off.

practice.stem: Scientists supplied one leaf of a cotton plant with carbon dioxide containing radioactive ¹⁴C. Aphids feeding on the stem were later removed, leaving their mouthparts (stylets) in the stem. Sap collected from stylets 72 cm below the leaf first contained ¹⁴C 1.5 hours after it was supplied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of movement of the ¹⁴C in the phloem, in cm h⁻¹.
parts.answer: 48 cm h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why aphid stylets are useful for studying the contents of sieve tubes.
parts.answer: The stylet penetrates a single sieve tube element; sap flows out under pressure without contamination from other cells, so pure phloem sap can be collected and analysed (and the flow shows the sap is under pressure).
parts.working: B1 enters one sieve tube/pure sap; B1 sap exudes under (hydrostatic) pressure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the structure of sieve tube elements allows rapid mass flow of sap.
parts.answer: Sieve tube elements have no nucleus, few organelles and only a thin layer of cytoplasm, so little resistance to flow; they are joined end to end into long tubes; the end walls are perforated as sieve plates with large pores.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: few organelles/no nucleus; thin cytoplasm; end to end/continuous tube; sieve plates with pores.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the apoplastic and symplastic pathways by which water crosses the cortex of a root.
parts.answer: Apoplast: water moves through the cell walls and spaces between cells, without crossing membranes. Symplast: water moves through the cytoplasm of cells, entering across the cell surface membrane and passing from cell to cell through plasmodesmata.
parts.working: B1 apoplast through cell walls/intercellular spaces; B1 symplast through cytoplasm; B1 via plasmodesmata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of the Casparian strip in the endodermis.
parts.answer: The Casparian strip is a band of suberin in the endodermis cell walls that is impermeable to water; it blocks the apoplast pathway, so water (and ions) must enter the cytoplasm/cross a cell surface membrane, allowing the plant to control which ions reach the xylem.
parts.working: B1 suberin/waterproof, blocks apoplast; B1 forces water through cytoplasm/membranes, control of ion uptake.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would increase the rate of transpiration from a wheat plant?
A a decrease in light intensity
B an increase in air humidity
C an increase in wind speed
D a decrease in air temperature
parts.answer: C an increase in wind speed
parts.working: Wind removes the humid layer of air near the stomata, making the water potential gradient between the air spaces and the outside air steeper. Higher humidity (B) reduces the gradient and so reduces transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water moves up the xylem from the roots to the leaves of a tall tree such as a chinar (Platanus orientalis).
parts.answer: Water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls into air spaces and diffuses out through stomata (transpiration); this lowers the water potential in the leaf, so water is drawn from the xylem; water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds (cohesion), so a continuous column is pulled up under tension; adhesion of water to the lignified xylem walls helps; this is the cohesion–tension mechanism / transpiration pull.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: evaporation/transpiration from leaves; water potential gradient; cohesion by hydrogen bonding; tension/pull on column; adhesion to xylem walls; continuous column.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the diameter of a tree trunk becomes slightly smaller during the hottest part of a sunny day.
parts.answer: Transpiration is fastest then, so tension in the xylem is greatest; the water column pulls the xylem walls inwards, so the trunk narrows.
parts.working: B1 high transpiration/high tension; B1 xylem walls pulled inwards.

practice.stem: A student set up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The capillary tube had an internal radius of 0.5 mm. An air bubble moved 45 mm along the tube in 5 minutes. The volume of a cylinder is πr²l.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7.07 mm³ min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of water uptake measured by the potometer is not exactly the same as the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Some water taken up is used in photosynthesis or to keep cells turgid/in cell growth; some water may be produced in respiration; so uptake is not equal to loss.
parts.working: B1 water used in photosynthesis/turgor; B1 so uptake ≠ water lost by evaporation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two precautions when setting up the potometer.
parts.answer: Any two of: cut the shoot under water; assemble the apparatus under water so no air enters; seal joints with petroleum jelly/check airtight; dry the leaves; allow the shoot to equilibrate before taking readings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: The rate of water loss from a potted maize plant was measured at 30 °C in a growth chamber at three relative humidities: 30 % – 4.6 g h⁻¹; 60 % – 2.9 g h⁻¹; 90 % – 0.8 g h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of relative humidity on the rate of water loss.
parts.answer: As humidity increases, rate of water loss decreases; the air outside the leaf contains more water vapour, so the water potential gradient (difference in water vapour concentration) between the air spaces and the outside air is smaller; so water vapour diffuses out of the stomata more slowly.
parts.working: B1 trend with figures; B1 smaller water potential/vapour gradient; B1 slower diffusion through stomata.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 90 % humidity, the rate of water loss fell close to zero. Suggest one disadvantage to the plant of a very low rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Less mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) carried to leaves in the transpiration stream / less evaporative cooling of leaves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During a dry spell in Sindh, maize plants closed their stomata during the afternoon. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of this.
parts.answer: Advantage: reduces water loss, so the plant does not wilt. Disadvantage: less CO₂ diffuses in, so the rate of photosynthesis falls (and leaves may overheat).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is found in mature xylem vessel elements?
A cytoplasm and a nucleus
B sieve plates
C lignified walls with pits
D plasmodesmata linked to companion cells
parts.answer: C lignified walls with pits
parts.working: Mature xylem vessel elements are dead, empty tubes with lignified walls and pits for lateral movement of water. Sieve plates (B) are found in phloem sieve tubes.

practice.stem: A student looked at a transverse section of a young sunflower stem and a transverse section of a young sunflower root under a light microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of the xylem and phloem in the stem.
parts.answer: In vascular bundles arranged in a ring near the outside of the stem; in each bundle xylem is on the inside (towards the centre) and phloem on the outside.
parts.working: B1 ring of vascular bundles; B1 xylem inner, phloem outer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of the xylem and phloem in the root.
parts.answer: In a central vascular cylinder (stele); xylem forms a central star/X shape with phloem in groups between the arms of the xylem.
parts.working: B1 central; B1 xylem star/cross shape with phloem between arms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tissue in the stem that lies between the epidermis and the vascular bundles.
parts.answer: Cortex (parenchyma; collenchyma may be present just below epidermis)
parts.working: B1 cortex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the structure of a mature xylem vessel element with a sieve tube element. Give three differences.
parts.answer: Xylem: dead/no cytoplasm; lignified walls; no end walls (continuous tube); pits; no companion cells. Sieve tube: living with thin cytoplasm (no nucleus); cellulose walls not lignified; sieve plates with pores; associated with companion cells; plasmodesmata.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct paired difference, up to three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how lignin in xylem walls helps the transport of water.
parts.answer: Lignin strengthens the walls so the vessels do not collapse under the tension of the water column; it also makes walls waterproof and helps adhesion of water.
parts.working: B1 prevents collapse under tension; B1 waterproof/adhesion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a companion cell is related to its function.
parts.answer: Many mitochondria – supply ATP for active transport/proton pumps; many plasmodesmata linking to the sieve tube element – allow sucrose to pass in and the companion cell to support the sieve tube; nucleus and dense cytoplasm/many ribosomes – carry out metabolic processes for the sieve tube element, which has no nucleus; cell surface membrane infolded (in some) – larger surface area for carrier/cotransporter proteins.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a feature linked to its function, up to four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a sieve tube element cannot survive without its companion cell.
parts.answer: The sieve tube element has no nucleus and few organelles/ribosomes, so it cannot make its own proteins or enough ATP; the companion cell provides these through plasmodesmata.
parts.working: B1 no nucleus/ribosomes, cannot make proteins; B1 companion cell supplies via plasmodesmata.

practice.stem: A student is asked to make a low-power plan diagram of a transverse section through a root of Ranunculus (buttercup), as seen through a light microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four rules the student should follow when drawing the plan diagram.
parts.answer: Any four of: draw no individual cells; use clear, continuous, sharp pencil lines; outline the different tissues only; draw in correct proportions; fill a large part of the space provided; no shading; label lines with a ruler that touch the tissue and do not cross; add a title/magnification if asked.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three tissues that should be labelled on the plan diagram.
parts.answer: Any three of: epidermis; cortex; endodermis; pericycle; xylem; phloem.
parts.working: 2 marks for three; 1 mark for two.

practice.stem: A student is asked to make a high-power drawing of a group of four adjacent cells from the palisade mesophyll layer of a leaf section. Each palisade cell contains many chloroplasts and has a large central vacuole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the features of a high-power drawing that an examiner would expect.
parts.answer: Exactly four cells drawn; each cell shared walls shown as double lines (cell walls of adjacent cells touching, showing both walls/middle lamella); cells drawn in correct proportion to each other and the size of the chloroplasts relative to the cells; chloroplasts drawn as outlines in the correct position (near the cell walls/surrounding the vacuole); clear unbroken lines, no shading; large drawing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two structures that should be labelled on one of the cells.
parts.answer: Any two of: cell wall; chloroplast; cytoplasm; vacuole/tonoplast (nucleus if visible).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Calotropis procera (aak) grows in the Cholistan and Thar deserts. Its leaves are thick, covered in a waxy layer and have many short hairs on both surfaces. It has a long, deep tap root.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the features described, explain how it helps the plant survive in a desert.
parts.answer: Thick waxy cuticle – reduces water loss by evaporation through the epidermis (cuticular transpiration); hairs – trap a layer of moist, still air near the stomata, reducing the water potential gradient so less water vapour diffuses out; deep tap root – reaches water deep in the soil/water table.
parts.working: 1 mark for each feature correctly explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other adaptations, not mentioned above, that xerophytic plants may have to reduce water loss.
parts.answer: Any two of: sunken stomata/stomata in pits; rolled leaves with stomata inside; fewer or smaller stomata; small leaves/spines (reduced surface area); stomata open at night (CAM).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which adaptation of a xerophytic leaf reduces transpiration mainly by keeping humid air close to the stomata?
A a thick waxy cuticle
B stomata in pits below the leaf surface
C a large number of stomata on the upper surface
D large air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
parts.answer: B stomata in pits below the leaf surface
parts.working: Sunken stomata trap still, humid air in the pit, reducing the water vapour gradient. A thick cuticle (A) reduces water loss across the epidermis itself rather than by humid air at the stomata.

practice.stem: Descriptions from a microscope slide set: Section X is roughly circular with a single ring of separate vascular bundles, each with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the outside, and a large central pith. Section Y is circular with a central core of xylem shaped like a four-armed star, phloem between the arms, an endodermis around the core and a wide cortex; there is no pith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which section is from a stem and which is from a root.
parts.answer: X is a stem; Y is a root.
parts.working: B1 both correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two observable differences between X and Y that support your answer, other than the presence of pith.
parts.answer: Any two of: vascular tissue in separate bundles in a ring (X) vs central stele (Y); xylem and phloem in same radius in X vs alternating in Y; endodermis visible in Y; xylem star shape in Y.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one feature that both sections have in common.
parts.answer: Both have xylem and phloem / epidermis / cortex.

practice.stem: A student compared two leaf transverse sections. Leaf P (from a bean plant grown in a well-watered garden) has a thin cuticle, a flat blade, stomata level with the surface on the lower epidermis and a spongy mesophyll with large air spaces. Leaf Q (from a desert grass) is rolled into a tube with the lower surface outside; it has a thick cuticle on the outer surface, stomata in grooves on the inner surface lined with hairs, and a compact mesophyll with small air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prepare a table to show three observable differences between leaf P and leaf Q.
parts.answer: Table with column headings 'feature', 'leaf P', 'leaf Q'; differences such as: shape – flat vs rolled; cuticle – thin vs thick; position of stomata – level on lower surface vs in grooves on inner surface; hairs – absent vs present; mesophyll air spaces – large vs small.
parts.working: B1 table with ruled columns and headings for both leaves and feature; 1 mark per correct difference, up to three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which leaf grows in a habitat with low water availability and give one reason from your table.
parts.answer: Leaf Q; e.g. rolled leaf traps humid air around stomata / thick cuticle.
parts.working: B1 Q with reason.

practice.stem: A student calibrated an eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer on which 1 division = 0.01 mm. At high power, 40 eyepiece graticule units lined up exactly with 25 stage micrometer divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule unit in µm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A xylem vessel measured 12 eyepiece units across at the same magnification. Calculate its actual diameter.
parts.answer: 75 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the graticule must be recalibrated if the student changes to a different objective lens.
parts.answer: The graticule scale stays the same size in the eyepiece but the specimen is magnified by a different amount, so each eyepiece unit represents a different actual length.

practice.stem: A student counted the stomata on the lower epidermis of a leaf of a guava tree in five fields of view at high power. The diameter of the field of view was 0.40 mm. Counts: 23, 19, 25, 21, 22.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of stomata per mm². Show your working and give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 175 per mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student drew a guard cell 60 mm long. The actual length of the guard cell was 150 µm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted stomata in five fields of view rather than one.
parts.answer: Stomata are not evenly spread over the leaf, so a mean of several fields gives a more representative/reliable estimate.

practice.stem: A student wants to investigate how wind speed affects the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot of a hibiscus plant. She has a bubble potometer, an electric fan with one speed, a metre rule, a stop-clock and an anemometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method she could use to carry out this investigation. Your method should allow her to collect valid and reliable data.
parts.answer: Any six of: cut the shoot under water and fit it to the potometer under water, airtight joints; vary wind speed by placing the fan at different distances (e.g. 25, 50, 75, 100, 125 cm) and measure the wind speed at the shoot with the anemometer; include a no-fan condition; allow the shoot to equilibrate for 5 min at each wind speed; measure the distance moved by the bubble in a set time (e.g. 5 min) with the scale/rule; reset the bubble with the reservoir; repeat at least three times at each distance and calculate a mean; keep light intensity (same lamp at fixed distance), temperature (fan may cool – monitor with thermometer) and humidity constant; use the same shoot throughout; convert distance to volume with πr²l and calculate rate per minute (per leaf area).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six valid points; detail must be specific.

practice.stem:
Four similar leaves were picked from a tree. Leaf A was untreated; leaf B had petroleum jelly on its upper surface; leaf C on its lower surface; leaf D on both surfaces. The leaves were hung up for 48 hours.
Initial mass / g: A 2.40, B 2.36, C 2.52, D 2.44
Final mass / g: A 1.62, B 1.65, C 2.37, D 2.38

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage loss in mass of each leaf. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 (initial − final)/initial × 100; A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why percentage loss is used rather than loss in mass.
parts.answer: The leaves had different starting masses, so percentages allow a fair comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what conclusions can be drawn from these results.
parts.answer: Most water is lost from the lower surface (blocking it reduced loss from 32.5 to 6.0 %); blocking the upper surface had little effect, so few stomata on the upper surface; the small loss from D shows a little water is lost through the cuticle/petroleum jelly or at the petiole; this suggests most stomata are on the lower surface.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three, with use of data in at least one.

practice.stem: A potted chilli plant with its pot sealed in a plastic bag was weighed every hour. Its mass fell from 486.2 g to 481.4 g in 6 hours. The total area of one surface of all its leaves was 240 cm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the pot and soil were sealed in a plastic bag.
parts.answer: So that water does not evaporate from the soil/pot; all mass lost is from the plant (transpiration).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss in mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 3.33 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the rate is given per cm² of leaf area.
parts.answer: So plants with different leaf areas/sizes can be compared.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot, using a potometer and a lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable, and how each would be measured or changed.
parts.answer: Independent: light intensity – changed by moving the lamp to different distances (or measured with a light meter). Dependent: rate of water uptake – distance moved by the air bubble in a set time.
parts.working: B1 IV with method; B1 DV with method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how two other variables should be standardised.
parts.answer: Temperature – place a heat filter/glass tank of water between lamp and shoot, or use an LED lamp, and monitor with a thermometer; humidity/air movement – carry out in a closed room with no draughts; use the same shoot/species and same leaf area.
parts.working: 1 mark for each variable with a method of control, up to two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lamp might affect the results in a way other than through light intensity.
parts.answer: A filament lamp releases heat, which increases temperature near the leaves and so increases evaporation/transpiration.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
A student measured the rate of transpiration of a potted plant at eight light intensities.
light intensity / klx: 5, 12, 20, 28, 35, 44, 52, 60
rate / cm³ h⁻¹: 0.8, 1.1, 1.0, 1.6, 2.1, 1.9, 2.6, 2.4
Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rs = 1 − (6Σd²) ÷ (n³ − n).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this test.
parts.answer: There is no correlation between light intensity and the rate of transpiration.
parts.working: B1 must say 'no correlation' (not 'no difference').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate rs. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 ranks correct (rate ranks 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 5, 8, 7); M1 Σd² = 6; A1 rs = 1 − 36/504 = 0.93.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of rs for n = 8 at p = 0.05 is 0.738. State a conclusion.
parts.answer: 0.93 > 0.738, so reject the null hypothesis; there is a significant positive correlation between light intensity and rate of transpiration.
parts.working: B1 compare/reject null; B1 significant positive correlation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the result does not prove that higher light intensity causes faster transpiration.
parts.answer: Correlation does not show cause; another factor that changed with light intensity (e.g. temperature, if a lamp was used) could cause the increase.

practice.stem: Celery stalks were placed with their cut ends in eosin (red dye) solution. One group was kept in bright light and another in the dark, both at 25 °C. After 30 minutes the dye had risen 9.5 cm in the light group and 2.0 cm in the dark group. Sections showed the dye only in small groups of cells near the outside of the stalk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the dye was found only in small groups of cells near the outside of the stalk.
parts.answer: The dye travels in the xylem; the xylem is in vascular bundles that are arranged near the outside (in a ring) in the stalk.
parts.working: B1 dye in xylem; B1 xylem in vascular bundles near outside.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the light and dark groups.
parts.answer: In light, stomata open; more water vapour diffuses out of the leaves (higher transpiration); greater tension/transpiration pull in the xylem, so water and dye are drawn up faster; in the dark stomata are mostly closed, so transpiration and pull are low.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: stomata open in light; more transpiration; greater tension/cohesion pull; stomata closed in dark.

practice.stem: A student will count open stomata on leaf epidermis peels taken from a bean plant at different light intensities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis that could be tested.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases, the percentage of open stomata increases (or a valid null hypothesis).
parts.working: B1 relates both variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sketch in words the shape of the graph you would predict, and give a biological reason.
parts.answer: The percentage of open stomata rises with light intensity then levels off (plateau) when nearly all are open; in light, guard cells take up K⁺ ions, water enters by osmosis and they become turgid, opening the pore.
parts.working: B1 rise then plateau; B1 reason linked to guard cell turgor/K⁺ uptake.

practice.stem: Two students used the same potometer and shoot to measure water uptake in still air. Student 1 took readings straight after setting up; student 2 waited 10 minutes. Their mean rates were 12.8 and 9.1 mm min⁻¹. Student 1 noticed small air bubbles appearing at the joint between the shoot and the rubber tubing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why student 1's results were higher and less reliable.
parts.answer: The shoot had not equilibrated to the conditions/stomata had not adjusted; air leaking in at the joint makes the bubble move further, giving an overestimate; (the shoot may have been under extra tension from being cut).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three improvements to the procedure to obtain more accurate and reliable results.
parts.answer: Any three of: cut the stem under water at a slant and fit it under water; seal joints with petroleum jelly and check for leaks; allow 5–10 min equilibration; measure at constant temperature/away from draughts; take at least three readings and calculate a mean, discarding anomalies; use a capillary of smaller radius for greater precision.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

subtopics.name: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

subtopics: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
parts.answer: mRNA for insulin is extracted from pancreatic β-cells; reverse transcriptase makes cDNA (no introns); sticky ends added / DNA cut with a restriction enzyme; plasmids cut with the same restriction enzyme; insulin gene and plasmid joined by DNA ligase (recombinant plasmid); plasmids taken up by bacteria (transformation); bacteria with the plasmid identified using a marker gene; cultured in a fermenter; insulin extracted and purified
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: mRNA from β-cells; reverse transcriptase → cDNA; restriction enzyme / complementary sticky ends; plasmid as vector cut with same enzyme; DNA ligase; promoter added; transformation (e.g. heat shock with Ca²⁺); marker gene (e.g. GFP) to identify transformed cells; cloning/culture in fermenter; extraction and purification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the role of each of the following in gene transfer: (i) restriction enzyme, (ii) DNA ligase, (iii) plasmid, (iv) sticky ends.
parts.answer: (i) cuts DNA at a specific base sequence (recognition site); (ii) joins sugar–phosphate backbones of DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds; (iii) vector that carries the gene into the host cell (and replicates there); (iv) short single-stranded overhangs that pair with complementary sticky ends by hydrogen bonding, so fragments join
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cDNA made from mRNA, rather than the gene cut from human chromosomes, is inserted into bacteria.
parts.answer: Human genes contain introns; bacteria cannot remove introns (no splicing), so the gene would not be expressed correctly; cDNA from mature mRNA has no introns
parts.working: 1 mark: genomic gene contains introns / cDNA does not. 1 mark: bacteria cannot splice out introns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the gene for green fluorescent protein (GFP) can be used as a marker to identify bacteria that have taken up a recombinant plasmid.
parts.answer: GFP gene is placed in the plasmid alongside the desired gene; bacteria that take up the plasmid express GFP; under ultraviolet (blue) light these colonies fluoresce green, so they can be identified and selected
parts.working: 1 mark each: GFP gene inserted with/next to the gene of interest (same plasmid); transformed bacteria make GFP; glow green under UV light / can be picked out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Antibiotic-resistance genes were once widely used as markers. Suggest two reasons why fluorescent markers are now often preferred.
parts.answer: Avoids spreading antibiotic resistance genes to other (pathogenic) bacteria; cells can be identified without killing non-transformed cells / no need for antibiotics; results seen quickly and easily
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible reasons.

practice.stem:
The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognises the sequence GAATTC and cuts between G and A on each strand, leaving sticky ends. One strand of a 43-nucleotide linear DNA molecule is:
5′ ATCGGAATTCTAGCCTAGGCATTACGGAATTCAGTTCAGCATG 3′

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of fragments produced when this DNA is cut with EcoRI.
parts.working: Two recognition sites (GAATTC at positions 5–10 and 27–32), so a linear molecule gives 3 fragments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the length, in nucleotides, of each fragment of the strand shown.
parts.answer: 5, 22 and 16 nucleotides
parts.working: Cuts after the G of each site (after nucleotides 5 and 27): 5, 27 − 5 = 22 and 43 − 27 = 16. 1 mark for two correct; 2 marks all three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must be used to cut the plasmid and the DNA containing the gene.
parts.answer: It produces complementary sticky ends on both; the sticky ends can base pair (hydrogen bond) with each other so ligase can join gene and plasmid
parts.working: 1 mark: same/complementary sticky ends. 1 mark: base pairing allows fragments to join before ligase seals them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bt cotton, widely grown in Pakistan, contains a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that codes for a protein toxic to caterpillars such as bollworms. Explain two benefits of growing Bt cotton.
parts.answer: Plants are protected from insect pests so yield increases; less insecticide spraying needed, which reduces costs for farmers and harm to the farmer's health and to non-target insects/environment; toxin is specific to certain insects
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: reduced crop damage/higher yield; less pesticide spraying; lower cost; less exposure of farm workers to sprays; fewer non-target organisms killed (beneficial insects); toxin is specific.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss two concerns about growing Bt cotton.
parts.answer: Pests may evolve resistance to the Bt toxin (selection), especially if refuges are not used; the gene may spread to wild relatives by pollen; seed is costly and must often be bought each year; other (secondary) pests not affected may increase; effects on non-target insects
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points, at least one explained (e.g. resistance: individuals with resistance alleles survive and reproduce, so allele frequency rises).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Golden rice has been genetically modified to produce β-carotene in its endosperm (the part of the grain that is eaten). The body converts β-carotene to vitamin A. Explain why the inserted genes are joined to a promoter that is active only in endosperm cells.
parts.answer: A promoter is needed for RNA polymerase to bind and transcribe the gene; an endosperm-specific promoter means the genes are expressed only in the grain (the eaten part), not wasting resources in leaves/roots
parts.working: 1 mark: promoter allows transcription (RNA polymerase binding). 1 mark: expression limited to endosperm/edible part.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why golden rice was developed and discuss one objection that has been raised against it.
parts.answer: Vitamin A deficiency causes blindness and weak immunity in children in countries where rice is the staple food; golden rice provides vitamin A cheaply in the normal diet. Objections: a varied diet/supplements could solve the problem; possible gene flow to other rice; concerns about control by companies or farmers' acceptance; unknown long-term effects
parts.working: 1 mark: vitamin A deficiency/blindness in rice-dependent populations. 1 mark: provides vitamin A in staple food. 1 mark: one objection explained.

practice.stem: A GM Atlantic salmon contains a growth hormone gene from another salmon species, joined to a promoter from a fish called the ocean pout. In one trial the GM salmon reached market mass in 18 months, compared with 36 months for non-GM salmon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the time to reach market mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the growth hormone gene was joined to a promoter from the ocean pout rather than its own promoter.
parts.answer: The normal promoter is only active in certain seasons/conditions; the ocean pout promoter is active all year, so growth hormone is produced continuously and the fish grow faster
parts.working: 1 mark: promoter controls when the gene is transcribed. 1 mark: pout promoter switched on all year → continuous growth hormone production.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The GM salmon are all sterile females and are farmed only in tanks on land. Explain why.
parts.answer: To prevent GM fish escaping and breeding with wild salmon; this avoids spreading the transgene into wild populations / GM fish outcompeting wild fish
parts.working: 1 mark: sterile so cannot reproduce if they escape. 1 mark: land tanks prevent escape; protects wild populations from gene flow/competition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the CRISPR–Cas9 system can be used to inactivate (knock out) a specific gene in a plant.
parts.answer: A guide RNA is made with a base sequence complementary to part of the target gene; it is combined with the Cas9 enzyme (a nuclease); the guide RNA base pairs with the target DNA, so Cas9 cuts both strands at that point; the cell repairs the break, often with errors (insertions/deletions), causing a frameshift so the gene no longer codes for a functional protein
parts.working: 1 mark each: guide RNA complementary to target sequence; Cas9 nuclease guided to site; cuts both DNA strands (double-strand break); repair introduces mutation / frameshift, inactivating gene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how CRISPR–Cas9 could instead be used to insert a corrected allele.
parts.answer: Supply a DNA template containing the desired allele with sequences matching either side of the cut; the cell uses this template to repair the break, so the new sequence is incorporated
parts.working: 1 mark: provide repair template with the correct sequence. 1 mark: template has ends matching the DNA around the cut, so it is used in repair.

practice.stem: A plasmid carries two antibiotic-resistance genes: one for ampicillin and one for tetracycline. A human gene is inserted into the middle of the tetracycline-resistance gene. After transformation, bacteria are spread on agar containing ampicillin and 200 colonies grow. The colonies are then copied, in the same positions, onto agar containing tetracycline; 46 colonies grow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing the colonies on the two types of agar allows bacteria containing the recombinant plasmid to be identified.
parts.answer: Only bacteria with a plasmid (either type) grow on ampicillin, because all plasmids carry the ampicillin-resistance gene; inserting the gene into the tetracycline-resistance gene inactivates it; so bacteria with recombinant plasmids grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline, while those with the original plasmid grow on both
parts.working: 1 mark each: ampicillin selects bacteria that took up any plasmid; insert disrupts tetracycline resistance gene; recombinant colonies are those that grow on ampicillin but fail to grow on tetracycline (replica plating).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of colonies on the ampicillin plate that contain the recombinant plasmid.
parts.working: M1: 200 − 46 = 154 colonies did not grow on tetracycline. A1: 154 ÷ 200 × 100 = 77 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a human glycoprotein hormone. It is produced commercially using genetically modified mammalian cells grown in culture rather than bacteria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: EPO has carbohydrate chains added after translation (in the Golgi body / ER); bacteria have no Golgi or ER so cannot add these chains; without them the protein may be inactive or quickly removed; mammalian cells modify the protein like human cells
parts.working: 1 mark each: EPO needs glycosylation/post-translational modification; bacteria lack ER/Golgi (cannot glycosylate); mammalian cells can produce the correctly modified/functional protein.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Before GM bacteria were used, diabetics were treated with insulin extracted from pigs and cattle. Give three advantages of insulin made by GM bacteria.
parts.answer: Identical to human insulin so fewer immune/allergic reactions; can be produced in large quantities to meet demand; cheaper/faster; no ethical or religious objections to animal source; no risk of transmitting animal diseases; consistent quality
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by a faulty gene for the enzyme ADA has been treated by gene therapy. Describe how this is done.
parts.answer: Stem cells (or T-lymphocytes) are taken from the patient's bone marrow/blood; a normal allele of the ADA gene is inserted into a virus vector (e.g. a retrovirus/lentivirus); the virus infects the cells and inserts the gene into their DNA; the modified cells are returned to the patient, where they produce ADA
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: cells removed from patient (bone marrow stem cells/T-cells); normal allele/functional gene; viral vector (retrovirus/lentivirus); gene inserted into cells' DNA; cells cultured and returned; cells now produce ADA so immune system works.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why gene therapy in humans is carried out on body (somatic) cells but not on egg, sperm or embryo cells.
parts.answer: Germ-line changes would be passed to future generations; who could not consent, and long-term effects are unknown (ethical concerns; not permitted in most countries)
parts.working: 1 mark: germ-line changes inherited by offspring. 1 mark: ethical issue – no consent / unknown effects / 'designer babies'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by genetic screening.
parts.answer: Testing a person's (or embryo's) DNA to find out whether they carry a particular allele, e.g. one that causes a genetic disease
parts.working: Testing DNA for presence of specific alleles/mutations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: β-thalassaemia is a recessive genetic disorder that is common in Pakistan. Suggest two ways in which genetic screening could be used to reduce the number of children born with β-thalassaemia.
parts.answer: Screening couples before marriage/pregnancy to find carriers so they can make informed decisions; prenatal testing of a fetus; screening embryos from IVF (pre-implantation genetic diagnosis) so only unaffected embryos are implanted
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: carrier screening of couples/relatives; prenatal diagnosis; embryo (PGD) screening with IVF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two ethical concerns about genetic screening.
parts.answer: Decisions to terminate pregnancies; stress/anxiety from results; confidentiality and discrimination (e.g. employers, insurance, marriage prospects); results may reveal information about relatives; could lead to selecting embryos for non-medical traits
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the use of viruses and liposomes as vectors for gene therapy.
parts.answer: Viruses enter cells efficiently and some insert genes into host DNA, so the effect is long-lasting; but they may trigger an immune response and may insert into/disrupt another gene. Liposomes (lipid spheres) fuse with cell surface membranes, cause little immune response and cannot cause infection; but they are less efficient at delivering genes and the gene is not integrated, so the effect is temporary
parts.working: Max 4: virus – efficient entry; may integrate (long-lasting); immune response; risk of insertional mutation. Liposome – fuses with membrane; little immune response/safe; less efficient; temporary expression.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Gene therapy for cystic fibrosis using liposomes in an inhaled spray must be repeated regularly. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The gene is delivered to epithelial cells lining the airways; these cells are short-lived and are replaced by new cells that do not carry the gene; the gene is not inserted into stem cells/host chromosomes
parts.working: 1 mark: airway epithelial cells are constantly replaced. 1 mark: new cells lack the gene / gene not integrated or passed on.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Screening shows that a husband and wife are both carriers of β-thalassaemia (heterozygous). Calculate the probability that their first child will have β-thalassaemia.
parts.working: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so P(tt) = 0.25.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that their first two children will both be unaffected. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1: P(unaffected) = 0.75 for each child (independent events). A1: 0.75 × 0.75 = 0.5625 → 0.56.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why marriages between close relatives (for example, first cousins) increase the chance of a child having a recessive disorder such as β-thalassaemia.
parts.answer: Relatives share many alleles inherited from common ancestors; so both partners are more likely to carry the same recessive allele, increasing the chance of a homozygous recessive child
parts.working: 1 mark: shared alleles from common ancestor. 1 mark: both more likely to be heterozygous for the same allele → more homozygous recessive offspring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In early gene therapy trials for one form of SCID, a retrovirus vector was used. Some of the treated children later developed leukaemia. Suggest how the gene therapy could have caused leukaemia.
parts.answer: Retroviruses insert their DNA at random positions in host chromosomes; in some cells the vector inserted next to/within a gene controlling cell division (proto-oncogene); this activated the gene (or disrupted a tumour suppressor gene), so the cell divided uncontrollably
parts.working: 1 mark each: random insertion into host DNA; inserted near a proto-oncogene/tumour suppressor gene; abnormal activation/disruption → uncontrolled mitosis (cancer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which the risks of this type of gene therapy could be reduced.
parts.answer: Use vectors that do not integrate (e.g. AAV or liposomes) or that integrate more safely (modified lentiviruses with self-inactivating promoters); use gene editing to correct the gene at its normal position; screen treated cells before returning them; monitor patients
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible suggestions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In one study, women with a harmful BRCA1 allele had a 72 % lifetime risk of breast cancer, compared with 12 % for women in the general population. Calculate how many times greater the risk was for women with the BRCA1 allele.
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of offering screening for harmful BRCA1 alleles to women whose relatives have had breast cancer.
parts.answer: Advantages: women with the allele can have more frequent checks so cancer is found early; can choose preventive treatment (e.g. surgery); relatives can be tested. Disadvantages: a positive result does not mean cancer will develop (risk not certainty), causing anxiety; a negative result does not rule out cancer; possible discrimination (insurance/employment/marriage); results affect relatives who did not choose testing; costly
parts.working: Max 3 for one side; need both sides for 4 marks. 1 mark each for valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps of one cycle of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), giving the approximate temperature of each step.
parts.answer: Denaturation at about 95 °C: hydrogen bonds break and the DNA strands separate; annealing at about 55–65 °C: primers bind (base pair) to complementary sequences at each end of the target sequence; extension at about 72 °C: Taq polymerase adds free nucleotides to the primers to build new complementary strands
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: 95 °C (90–98 °C) denaturation; strands separate/H bonds broken; 50–65 °C annealing of primers to complementary sequences; 72 °C extension; Taq polymerase adds nucleotides from primer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Taq polymerase, from a bacterium living in hot springs, is used in PCR.
parts.answer: It is thermostable – it is not denatured at 95 °C; so it does not need to be replaced after every cycle, and its optimum temperature is about 72 °C
parts.working: 1 mark: not denatured at high (95 °C) temperature. 1 mark: does not need to be added each cycle / works at 72 °C.

practice.stem: A forensic scientist has a sample containing 50 copies of a target DNA sequence from a hair root found at a crime scene in Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of copies of the target DNA after 25 cycles, assuming the number doubles in every cycle. Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each cycle takes 3 minutes. Calculate the total time for 25 cycles.
parts.answer: 75 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why two different primers are needed.
parts.answer: Each primer is complementary to the 3′ end of one of the two strands of the target sequence; DNA polymerase needs a primer to start adding nucleotides; using one for each strand means both strands are copied and only the region between them is amplified
parts.working: 1 mark: one primer per strand (strands have different sequences/are antiparallel). 1 mark: polymerase needs a primer to start / defines the region copied.

practice.stem:
A DNA profile was used in a family court case. Bands (fragment lengths in kilobases, kb) were:
child: 1.2, 2.5, 3.1, 4.0, 5.6
mother: 1.2, 3.1, 4.8, 6.0
man X: 2.5, 4.0, 5.6, 7.2
man Y: 2.5, 3.9, 6.0, 8.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments.
parts.answer: DNA is negatively charged (phosphate groups), so in an electric field it moves towards the positive electrode (anode); the gel acts as a sieve/mesh; smaller fragments move more easily and travel further in a given time
parts.working: 1 mark each: negative charge on phosphates; moves to anode/positive terminal; smaller fragments move faster/further through gel pores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which man could be the biological father. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Man X; the child's bands that are not from the mother (2.5, 4.0 and 5.6 kb) all match bands of man X, but man Y lacks the 4.0 and 5.6 kb bands
parts.working: 1 mark: man X. 1 mark: all non-maternal bands of the child are present in man X (man Y lacks two of them).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why DNA sequencing of a disease-causing gene can give more information than a DNA profile.
parts.answer: Sequencing shows the exact order of bases, so a specific mutation (e.g. a single base change) can be identified; a profile only shows fragment lengths
parts.working: Exact base sequence revealed / identifies specific mutations.

practice.stem:
A DNA ladder was run alongside a PCR product. Distances moved by the ladder bands from the well:
1000 bp: 12 mm | 500 bp: 24 mm | 250 bp: 36 mm | 125 bp: 48 mm
The PCR product moved 30 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the ladder to estimate the size of the unknown fragment. Give your answer to the nearest base pair.
parts.answer: 354 bp
parts.working: M1: each extra 12 mm halves the size (size = 1000 ÷ 2^((d − 12)/12)). M1: unknown at 30 mm is 18 mm beyond the 1000 bp band, so 1000 ÷ 2^1.5. A1: 1000 ÷ 2.828 = 353.6 → 354 bp. (Allow 350–360 bp read from a semi-log graph for 2 marks.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a ladder of fragments of known size is run in a separate lane of the same gel.
parts.answer: Distance moved depends on conditions (voltage, time, gel concentration), so the ladder must experience the same conditions; it gives a calibration to compare the unknown with
parts.working: 1 mark: same conditions/same gel and run time. 1 mark: allows size of unknown to be determined by comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a microarray can be used to compare the genes being expressed in cancer cells and in normal cells from the same tissue.
parts.answer: mRNA is extracted from each type of cell; reverse transcriptase makes cDNA, labelled with a different fluorescent dye for each sample (e.g. red for cancer, green for normal); the cDNA is added to the microarray, where it hybridises (base pairs) with complementary DNA probes for thousands of genes; unbound cDNA is washed off; the array is scanned and the colour/intensity of each spot shows which genes are expressed in which sample
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mRNA extracted; converted to cDNA; fluorescent labels (two colours); hybridisation to complementary probes on the chip; washing; scanning – colour/intensity shows expression level.

practice.stem:
Researchers compared gene expression in leaves of drought-stressed and well-watered wheat plants using a microarray. cDNA from drought-stressed plants was labelled with a red dye and cDNA from watered plants with a green dye. Mean intensities (arbitrary units):
gene P: red 1200, green 300
gene Q: red 400, green 400
gene R: red 150, green 600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of red to green intensity for each gene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your ratios, describe the expression of each gene in the drought-stressed plants compared with the watered plants.
parts.answer: P is expressed four times more in drought-stressed plants (switched on/up-regulated); Q is unchanged; R is expressed four times less (down-regulated)
parts.working: 1 mark: P up-regulated, R down-regulated. 1 mark: Q unchanged, with use of the factor of four.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment should be repeated with samples from several plants.
parts.answer: Individual plants vary; repeats show whether the differences are consistent/reliable (and allow statistical testing)
parts.working: Natural variation between plants; check reliability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A short gene sequence of 60 bases from a newly discovered bacterium was compared with the matching sequence of a known species using a database search. The sequences differed at 9 positions. Calculate the percentage identity of the two sequences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by bioinformatics and outline how databases of DNA and protein sequences can be used to identify an unknown pathogen.
parts.answer: Bioinformatics is the collection, storage and analysis of biological data (e.g. sequences) using computers; the sequence of the unknown organism is entered into a search program; it is compared/aligned with sequences in the database; the most similar sequences suggest the identity or closest relatives of the pathogen
parts.working: 1 mark: definition (computer storage/analysis of biological information). 1 mark: unknown sequence compared/aligned with database sequences. 1 mark: closest match identifies organism/relationship.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why comparing a longer sequence would give a more reliable result.
parts.answer: A short sequence may match several species by chance / gives fewer differences to compare; longer sequences give more data so the comparison is more accurate
parts.working: More bases compared, chance matches less important.

practice.subtopic: Skill: statistics (SD, SE, CI, t-test, Spearman, chi-squared)
practice.stem:
An agricultural researcher in Punjab compared seed-cotton yield per plant (g) for Bt cotton and non-Bt cotton grown in the same field.
Bt cotton: n = 10, mean = 92.4 g, standard deviation = 8.1 g
non-Bt cotton: n = 10, mean = 81.7 g, standard deviation = 9.3 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a null hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference between the mean yield per plant of Bt cotton and non-Bt cotton
parts.working: Must refer to no (significant) difference in mean yield between the two varieties.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of t, using t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The critical value of t at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10. Explain what your result shows.
parts.answer: 2.74 is greater than 2.10, so the null hypothesis is rejected; there is a significant difference in mean yield (the difference is unlikely to be due to chance, p < 0.05)
parts.working: 1 mark: compares calculated t with critical value (greater). 1 mark: reject null hypothesis / difference is significant (not due to chance).

practice.stem: A student transformed E. coli with 0.05 µg of plasmid carrying a GFP gene and an ampicillin-resistance gene. After heat shock, the bacteria were mixed with nutrient broth to a total volume of 1000 µl. 100 µl of this mixture was spread on an agar plate containing ampicillin, and 380 glowing colonies grew.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of transformed cells produced in the 1000 µl mixture.
parts.working: 100 µl gave 380 colonies, so 1000 µl contains 380 × 10 = 3800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Transformation efficiency is the number of transformed cells per µg of plasmid DNA. Calculate the transformation efficiency. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 7.6 × 10⁴ transformants per µg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why only 100 µl of the mixture, rather than all of it, was spread on the plate.
parts.answer: So that colonies are separate/countable (not overlapping)
parts.working: Too many colonies would merge and could not be counted.

practice.stem:
Three lines of GM rice (A, B and C) carrying genes for β-carotene synthesis were grown together with non-GM rice. β-carotene content of the grain was measured in three samples from each line (µg per g of grain):
non-GM: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 (mean 0.0)
line A: 1.4, 1.9, 1.5 (mean 1.6)
line B: 6.2, 7.5, 6.8 (mean 6.8)
line C: 21.0, 28.5, 36.0 (mean 28.5)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student concludes that line C is the best line to grow for vitamin A. Using the data, discuss the extent to which this conclusion is supported.
parts.answer: Support: line C has the highest mean β-carotene (28.5 µg/g), about four times line B; its range does not overlap with A or B. Against: line C has the largest variation (range 21.0–36.0), so results are less consistent; only three samples per line; plants grown in one place/season only; β-carotene content is not the same as vitamin A delivered (losses in storage/cooking, absorption); yield and other traits not measured; no statistical test done
parts.working: 1 mark: highest mean quoted. 1 mark: no overlap with other lines / clear difference. Max 2 limitations from: large spread in C; small sample (3); one site/season; β-carotene may be lost in storage/cooking; yield/taste not considered; no statistical test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the non-GM rice was included.
parts.answer: As a control to show that β-carotene is produced because of the inserted genes (non-GM rice has none)
parts.working: Control/comparison showing the effect is due to the genetic modification.

practice.stem:
A student ran PCR to amplify one gene from the DNA of a chickpea plant, using different annealing temperatures. Products were run on a gel. Results:
50 °C: strong band of correct size plus three other bands
55 °C: one strong band of correct size
60 °C: one strong band of correct size
65 °C: one faint band of correct size
70 °C: no bands

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why no product was formed at 70 °C.
parts.answer: At high temperature the hydrogen bonds between primer and template are unstable / break, so the primers cannot remain base-paired (anneal) to the template; without primers Taq polymerase cannot start making new strands
parts.working: 1 mark: primers cannot anneal / hydrogen bonds not stable at 70 °C. 1 mark: polymerase needs bound primer to begin extension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why extra, unexpected bands appeared at 50 °C.
parts.answer: At low temperature primers can bind to sequences that are only partly complementary (mismatches tolerated, some hydrogen bonds still form); so other regions of DNA are also copied, giving products of different lengths
parts.working: 1 mark: primers bind to partly complementary/non-target sites. 1 mark: other DNA regions amplified, giving different-sized fragments.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the best annealing temperature from these results and give a reason.
parts.answer: 55–60 °C, because a single strong band of the correct size was produced
parts.working: 55 or 60 °C (or between) with reason: single, strong correct band.

practice.stem: A class in Peshawar used gel electrophoresis to compare DNA fragments from three plant samples. Several groups reported that: bands were smeared, some lanes were empty, the smallest fragments were not visible, and different groups obtained different band positions for the same sample. The method: wells were made with a comb before the gel had fully set; samples were added with a dropper; the gel was run at a high voltage for 2 hours; no DNA ladder was used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of error in this procedure that could explain the poor results, and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Samples loaded unevenly / overflowing wells → use a micropipette with fresh tips and load the same volume carefully; gel run too long so small fragments ran off → run for a shorter time / check with loading dye; voltage too high causing smearing/overheating → use a lower voltage; DNA degraded/contaminated → use fresh samples/sterile equipment; wells damaged → let the gel set fully before removing comb; no ladder → include a DNA ladder
parts.working: 1 mark for each error linked to the observations (max 2) and 1 mark for each matching improvement (max 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between repeatability and accuracy in this investigation.
parts.answer: Repeatability: getting the same band pattern when the procedure is repeated; accuracy: how close the estimated fragment sizes are to the true sizes
parts.working: 1 mark each correct definition applied to the context.

practice.stem: A student plans to investigate how the duration of heat shock at 42 °C (0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90 s) affects the uptake of a plasmid containing GFP and ampicillin-resistance genes by E. coli. Transformed bacteria are spread on ampicillin agar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable, and state how the dependent variable would be measured.
parts.answer: Independent: duration of heat shock (s); dependent: transformation efficiency / number of colonies (glowing colonies) on the plate, counted after incubation (e.g. 24 h at 37 °C)
parts.working: 1 mark: IV and DV correctly named. 1 mark: DV measured by counting (fluorescent) colonies after fixed incubation time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how three other variables should be controlled.
parts.answer: Temperature of heat shock kept at 42 °C using a thermostatically controlled water bath; same mass/volume of plasmid DNA added (using a micropipette); same volume and concentration of bacteria (same culture, same optical density); same time on ice before and after; same volume spread and incubation temperature/time
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three variables each with a method of control (variable alone = 0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control and explain its purpose.
parts.answer: Bacteria treated in the same way but with no plasmid added; shows that colonies arise only from transformation (no growth on ampicillin/no glowing)
parts.working: No-plasmid (or no heat shock) control with purpose.

practice.stem: Ecologists want to know whether pollen from Bt maize, which drifts onto wild plants beside fields, harms the caterpillars of a butterfly that feeds on those plants. Caterpillars will be fed leaves dusted with Bt maize pollen, leaves dusted with non-Bt maize pollen, or leaves with no pollen, and survival after 7 days recorded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State a hypothesis that the investigation could test.
parts.answer: Caterpillars fed on leaves dusted with Bt maize pollen have a lower survival rate than those fed on leaves with non-Bt pollen (or: Bt maize pollen reduces survival of these caterpillars)
parts.working: Testable statement linking pollen type to survival.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null hypothesis.
parts.answer: There is no significant difference in survival between caterpillars fed on leaves with Bt pollen and those fed on leaves with non-Bt pollen
parts.working: No significant difference in survival between the groups.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the results if Bt toxin in pollen harms these caterpillars, and explain why caterpillars fed on leaves with no pollen should also be included.
parts.answer: Prediction: survival lower (and growth slower) in the Bt pollen group than in the non-Bt pollen group. The no-pollen group shows whether pollen itself (not the toxin) affects survival / gives a baseline
parts.working: 1 mark: correct directional prediction. 1 mark: no-pollen control separates effect of pollen from effect of toxin.
